(Hear hear.) Whenever he found that Sir Gilbert Greenill or his supporters were ad- Vacating what ho coasidered a false principle be should de- nounce that with all the power 'he bad at his command, but so far as his opponent was personallV e'tncerned he desired to have nothing at all said against him iii any., way.,l Hear. hear.) e.He Male not claim a reciprocity of that feeling from their opponents, for be knew that as a young elec- tioneerer he was more liable -td attacks than a veteran in politics Bitch air his opponent was, and in enterininto the fight he certainly exoec,ed .he should receive some - rubs, and be had no &inlet, some hard knock. . but he hoped, that when the day of vic- tory ewe be should find that there were no scratches that would, leave any mark at all. ' (Loud • applause.) As be said. .he must not expect a reciprocity of that 'consideration', and he already had reason to knew that he ninit look.for,criticlem. He had already been' at- laded to in lhatgreat oveilloweineeting which was held at the Red Lion the other night. Ho was spoken of personally by one of the oratots at that meeting. The gentleman had the candour to say that he had never seen him (Mr. Croe; field), but he had'fotmed the opinion that his oratoryviould not enlighten' the'House of Commons. - Well, when be was waited on by a deputation with a view to that candida- ture he was asked a great many questions, bathe was bound to say the question of oratory never seemed to enter into the consideration of the gentlemen who honoured him by their visit. (Hear, hear.) He claimed to have the power of speech—(hear, hear)—he did not say the gift of speech— : ' he drew that distinction—and he was afraid many of them I would remember what ha feared were the many rather dreary ' nights they spent together last winter. ("No, no," and ap- plause.) He hoped, however, that he conveyed to them the impression that he was not then approaching politics for the first time. (Hear, heat) He had had dreams of what his parliamentary duties might be after the day of victory. He had had many such emanate but in, hi wildest imagination he bad never ,pictureelehimeelf standing in the House of Commons claiming their attention to his oratory. No, if it was a necessity that( the member for Warrington should have oratorY one or other of them must retire. (Hear, hear, end loud laughter.) - If there was any gentleman present who had come into that room expecting to hear an oratorical treat he warned him at once that 'he might out with his nightcap and take 'a nap, but to be sure to wake up in time to hear their friend Mr, Percy. (Applause.) And after all what was the use of oratory? His opieion of the House of Commons was rather that of a business assembly, where I men who had ideas were content simply to express them in few words awl have done with it, endmot waste the weary moments, and weary hours, and weary days and nights, as was done in some cases by repeating the same thine over and over again, very often in the self-same words. (Hear, heart) The other day he had had the pleasure of spending some few hours with one of those tine . old Liberals ,who were in the House of Commons when oraterkeof Mr. Robert Davies' standard were counted by dozens in • the House of Commons. ghat gentleman told him i a very interesting story which he would relate, but before ' that he would tell them the name of his friend for it added influence to the testimony he was about to give—he was speaking of Mr. John Cheetbam, who in the old times represented the south division of the ccinnty of Lancashire before being divided as now. Mr. Cheethatreat the age Of 81. is delightirg his friends by talking of his old reminis- cences. He told him (Mr. Crosfield) the other day that he remembered only once having his vote changed in the coerce of a debate in the House of Commons, and it was by A eery :Ample circumstance. A question of great interest was being debated, and the Government was likely to loose the vote that was going to be taken, and they sent for an orator to come and save them from the dilemma. They called to their assistance Mr. Macauley, one of the most brilliant speakers in the House of Commons that had been / there within the memory of living men, and he mareV/hat was called a great oration, and Mr. Cheetham acknowledged he changed;bis opinion. It wag, however, not the oratory that did it; it was the simple statement of a simple fact, which showed the absurdity •f the position in which Mr. Cheatham was,going to place himself. (Hear, bear, and applause.) It 'u that'brief 20 words that changed his opinion, net the brilliance of the oratory. (Hear, hear.) He (Mr. Cresfield) did not hope to into the House of Commons as a , Macauley but he did hope that if he ever had the oepor- , tunity of making his voice heard in the House of Commons it Would be to express shorteterse common sense. (liear, hear, and applause.) He was told by the same person at the Red Lion—at least he thought it was he who said that : he (Mr. Crosfield) was there only as a name. He could not help carrying his mind back to eighteen mouths ago When he appeared fn that room for the first time, inviting but a fen valued friends in Warrington, he acknowledged to feel- ing that be was but a name. ' Bu f the experience of these eighteen tnontbs bad shown bite that be hadenewevery many valued friends in Warrington. and that to them he I was something mere than a name. (Loud Lapplauge.) But there wae something after all in n name, when that name ' was a good one -- (loud applause)— and he hoped that when he bad the honour of Mr. Roberta Davietes icquaintance, and When be might' have the opportunity of representing him, though it might be unwillingly to himself —(laughter)—that at the termination of their acquaintance Mr. Hilbert Davies Would have to acknowledge that he done nothing to dishonour a name, which be believed to Mr. t Davies was a name of honourse sed, one which he himself liaadusree) Re e had to hold i n already measdteeemhis (allea.i hear, i and ap- plause.) been delivered en-Thursday MorhingPefong la Zejiir his opponent. 'lt wasiaow on the wallculhe hoped they had all read it. (Hear, hear, and aroplape) eilui.teughed t upon many subjects; be could not claim that 'he had' dealt wadi,tihrert ,ewmo.re vßaugtue.h e isvw aesl l ,t owldhetn-hahtethcaemuetterroancioeoskof,atrhhart , vast sphere of suejects that was open to him, he felt it was utterly impossible to deal.with any one thing in anything like an exhaustive mermen 'Hp therefore felt- there was no option between suggesting various subjects which', had to be' dealt with or dealing with one fully, and he thought the former was the better way rather than the letter. (Hear, hear.) He might certainly have expressed his full views on some of the subjects to which he had alluded, but he hoped they would believe him when he said that modesty had throughout life always stood in his way, and he felt that if he as a new candidate, -and as a possible young member of the House of Commonsestiould tell them what he' was going to do in the way, of , these various worms, they might aft.r all call him a humbug when he ,got into the House of Commons and found that he hid not the power to carry out those ideas, he 'ha'd noticed. He 'honed that in the course at next Month ise(y) uld be able to' explain to them and convince them that his views on those questions were right. (Applause.) They would meet one 'another very frequently, and he should have-a greatedeal to say to them before they parted. (Applause.) On the ,-, ,(-'v ',Kfigel'aVt• .

ASSAULT BY A GAMEKEEPER. John Broady, a game- keeper, in the emoky of Mr. Lyon, Stratton, was charged with assaulting a carter named Charles Skinner, Admiral= street, Warrington, and employed by Messrs. Pairclough, of Warrington, on thc 28th September, at Appleton. There was a cross-sfnituons taken out.—Mr. Arthur Browne ap- peared for the complainant, and Mr: Percy Davies for the defendant.—lt was stated that the ~complainant and a man .named SAO born were going .along Stratton-road, tear Mr. Lyon's gate at Appleton, with a horse and cart. when be dog went.through a gate on to land belonging to Mr;Ly on. Broady was some distance in front with a gun, and when he saw the dpgUri the land, he came towards the two men at a good pace' and asked whose dog it was. Complainant re. plied, "Well, it's mine if it's anybody's." Defendant then ,said be would summon him, and asked him his name, to which •CoreplainAnt replied that his name was anything. After a short altercation Broody caught hold of complainant by the whiskers, and struck him on the left cheek, and bit him on the head with the barrel of his gun, "raising a lump as big 1 as a hen's egg." Skinner took hold of the gun, the muzzle ' being turned towards his stomach. Broady having re- , gained posseesion of the gun went into the middle of the road, it was stated by complainant, and threatened to let them have the contents of the grin.—la defence, Broady denied having struck the complainant, and alleged that the row had been cornmcnced by Skinner.—The magistrates thought that Broady was the aggressor, and fined mm 20s and costs, in all £2 7s ed.. He would only say Brooks, of Warrington, a resolution pledging the meeting to what Mr. Percy said, that all the reforms which the Liberal support Sir Richard was carried. party had passed during the past 50 years beginning with the emancipation of the Catholics and ending with the Re- distribution Bill, bad been passed in spite of the strenuous opposition of the Tories. (Hear, hear, and applause.) What amused him a good deal just at present was that the Tory party claimed that they had been the author of all these reforms. (Laughter.) It was a wonder to him against whom they had been contending for 40 or 50 years. (Hear, bear, and laughter.) Whom had they been fighting against? Had they been beating the air? Had the opposi- tion that they thought was made to them been a phantom of their own imagination? He thought not. (Applatmee) At any rate, if the Tories had been so much in favour of the reforms which he contended the Liberals had passed they had disguised their opinions very successfully. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) . If they had loved them why had they dissembled their lone until it was actually thought they had a strong desire to kick them downstairs? (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Hewes not going to detain them, hecouee those subjects on which he might have spoken had really been exhausted by Mr. Percy, and he had only to say to them, let them be in earnest, let them work hard, let them give a long pull, a strong pull, and a pull altogether, and they would place that hoeough in the position of an impregnable Liberal fortress, inYncible for the future. (Loud applause.) The resolution was then caeried enthusiastically. Mr. PEARSON said they should lock to them in Warring- ton from the dense darkness of Liverpool for the enlighten- ment and the hope and the success which they would' most assuredly give them. (Applause.) Referring to Mr. Ashmead Bertlett's speech at Warrington, Mr. Pearson said it seemed to him that that gentleman was playing with the edged weapon of protection. If he promised anything, and if the Tory party promised anything at the present moment, it was that if they were allowed to inquire into the cause of bad trade, they would in their turn do what they could to reverse the policy of free trade. (Hear, hear.) Mr. W. CROSFIELD groomed a vote of thanks to the Chairman and Mr. Percy. (Applause.) Mr.'Joun CROSFIELD, in seconding this proposal, said he should like to relieve himself a little—(laughtere—of some of the feelings that had been excited in him already, in the early port of that election. There was one thing that their Tory friends c)ald beat them at, and that was " cheek.' (Hear, hear, and loud laughter.) They said and did some of the most impertinent thinee he ever remembered in his life; and it appeared they never mended. (Laughter.) At the last election they were full of their cheek, and they talked as if the Liberals had no right to an existence, and the same spirit was amongst them now. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) On Friday morning he got the address of Sir G. Greenall—(laughter)—which was very interestieg of course, and he got with it a letter signed by Mr. Sylvanus Reynolds. (" Cheek,'' and laughter.) At the bottom of that letter was a postscript " On no account ,be tempted to promise your vote t 3 any canvasser for the Liberal candi- date." (Loud laughter.) Well, he thought that was a very pretty thing for him to receive on Friday morning— (laughter)—and when he met his friend‘. Sylvanue Rey- nolde he should thank him for that. (Lan, er.) But he should like to see a Tory canvasser conung Olm for his vote, that was all. (Loud laughter.) Well. th' had had a great deal of food given to them that night, hat if ethey would allow him he should like to touch upon tine point. ("Go on," and applause.) Thera was one very irAyortant question that had agitated a great many minds in Chit part, and that was the question of education. (Hear hear.' He wanted them to understand that he believed denotninationel echools were as worthy of support as school board schools. (Hear, hear, and applause,) He said it was a great credit 'to Warrington that the different denominations had built their own schools and educated their Own children without the aid of a school board, and he hoped he should' never live to see the day wlfien there was a eohool board in War- rington. (Hear, hear.) He would tell them what wanted remedying, and what he trusted his cousin and Mr. Percy would see done when they went to Parliament, and that was that town councils should have the sense power given to them as a school board. If that was done they should get rid of those grievances of poor people having to go before the Board of Guardians. (Hear, hear.) It was a. credit to the working classes that they would not go to that Bastille, and they ought not to be put to the humiliation of going before the Board of Guardians to get their school fees when they were ill or out cif work. (happlause.) He therefore held that town councils ought to have as much power in that way as any school board, and if Mr. Forster had taken the sensible advice of that great statesman, John Bright— (applause)—he would have included that in his bill. He (Mr. Crosfield) knew that Mr. Bright advised Mr. Forster to give that power to town cement's and he would not do it. (Hear, hear.) Well, the different denominations in Warring- ton bad built their own schools, and were just as much en- titled to have them supported by the State as any school board—(hear, hear)—and he was thankful that their candi- date was of the same opinion, and that all denominations might depend upon this, that they would have perfect liberty to teach and do in their schools as they liked. They were all for freedom in religion and for religious equeAity. (Applause) That was a subject that had been agitating a good many minds, and he hoped those few words be had said would set their minds at rest. (Hear, hear.) He was glad to see such a meeting that night, and he hoped that all their ward meetings would be as well attended. He men- tioned that in the South-West Ward a meeting would be held in the Co-operative Hall on the 10th November, and he had got his friend Mr James Samuelson, the working men's candidate in Liverpool, to come and address them. (Loud applause.) The resolution was carried with acclamation. The CHAIRMAN and Mr. ?SECT briefly responded, and the meeting ended.

SIR GILBERT GREENALL ON TIIE ELECTION. A meeting or the supporters of the Conservative candle date was held in St. Peter's school, John-street, Warrington, on Tuesday evening. The chair Was occupied by Coun- cillor Francomb, and amongst those also present were Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart,, Mr. Gilbert Greenall, Mr Henry Greenall, Capt. Reynolds, J.P.S Mr. John White, J.P., and others.—The Chairman haying made an introductory speech, Mr. T. Cawley proposed, and Mr. R. Isherwood seconded the following resolution, which was carried : " That this meeting pledges itself to use all legal and just means to return as representative for Warrington at the coming election, Sir Gilbert Greenall, who has ever proved' himself to be a consistent Conservative, and has on all oc- casions manifested a deep interest in all that concerns the prosperity of Warrington." Sir.Crieneuz GRISENALL then addressed the meeting. He said: friends and gentlemen,—l an here amengst you, and I have no other feeling, I have no other intention than to express plainly what I feel, and as distinctly to say what I shall consider it my duty to do. (Hear,. hear.) Now do not misunderstand me. (Hear, hear.) lam by feeling, I was going to say by nature, a free man. ram an independent man. (Appeases.) I have nothing to gain from others. All that I have to gait: is the satisfac- tion of having done my duty, and coupled with that satis- faction your good opinion. (Applause ) New, my friends, you have me entirely. I have turned rnyeel f, as it were, to your observation inside out. I hive nothing to reserve, nothing to conceal from you, and questione that You ask-me shall be answered straightforwardly, and what. I say—God giving me grace to stand to my reso- lutions—what I say shall and will be true. (Applause.) Well, the day is come; the time is arrived ; I was looking forward to it. I wished this day to corns. Iwish oar contest to be on. I wish to know whether the inhabi- tants of the town of Warrington wish to be represented by those who have dragged the trade of this country dawn to nothing, (Hear, hear.) Do they wish to be rep enented by theme who have suffered the honour and the glory of lenglend to dwindle, or do they wish to be represented by those who will clearly declare their policy, and what they are doing. and leave the people of England to judge of their words by their actions. (Applause.) Well, something has been said about an address. I have only to do with my own address. My own address was not written thoughtlessly. It was not written without consideration. It was not written to throw I dust in the eyes of short-sighted men, (Applause.) It was written as the plain embodiment and enunciation of my opinions—(heer, hear)— and .svery line written there, every wort expressed there, Gilbert Greenall will stand by. Well, / will not detain you long. I do not like to speak upon subjects that are rather personal. But I roust say this It. was my honour to represent this town for some years. I represented it when I was your member faithfully. (Hese, hate) I did that which I always intended to do. I'was always just to the working-man. My object ever was, as it is now, as far as I am ale, to take care that no legislation shall ever oppress the working-man. My desire is to see master and man equal before the slaw. They were not until lately, and they were made equal by a measure of our frieed' Sir Richard Cross. (Applause.) In the matter of compen- sation for injuries, the working-man and tee master now stand before the same court. They ought to do. I have always approved, strongly approved., of the legislation which gave compensation for injuries done to working-men. I wish that Act of Parliament to be cerried out in its en- actments and in its provisions, and I wish that that act shall be made what it is net at pre- sent but if it be made as I would have it made it will be better for the working-man. I wish that Act to be made compulsory. (Hear, hear.) Well, for one moment. We were not as successful in the year 1883 as we intend to be in the year 188.5. I did not like our de- feat then I say unhesitatingly that our defeat, and the way it was done—that those who succeeded in gaining the palm had neither !armour, respectability, or glory attached to their victory. (Applause.) My desire was to have applied to Parliament for an investigation into the proceed- ings. lam quite, quite sure if that application had been made and we had a commissioner, as sure as I ant now speaking—quite as sure—the seat would have had to be given up. (Hear, hear.) Well, what then ?' lam grieved to think that I might not have renvered the seat. It was a most unfortunate thing. My directions and my orders were that those who represented me should take care to keep within the four corners of the law, and if we had a petition, and our opponent had done wrong, we shoad have hadiour ease against it. Well. when the termination of that election came, I was quite satisfied that upon a• petition. Mr. Mc- Minutes would not retain the seat. I think so now,.and I am sure of it. (Applause.) But we might not have secured the seat. I must say that some friends are too good friends. (Hear, hear) Some of my friends were injudicious and had committed email matters—small matters, compared with what was done—had committed small matters which would not have given us the seat, and I therefore thought it was better in every respect that we should,nothave•the ex- citement and the trouble of an election. But I vraEo always determined and resolute, .if we stood together. that either in my person or in the person of some other CenserYative gentleman the borough should be reserved. I believe we now have the opportunity. (Hear, hear.) Well, I ant anxious to speak very, very, free indeed,, as far as what concerns myself; very free. I well considered, what it was my duly to do. Two parties. were to be con- sidered on the question of dutv. What was my- duty to you and what was my duty to., myself ? Well, lam not ashamed that I am a somewhat old man, but I assnre you here that I weighed that truth well over, and if I had felt that I had net sufficient strength and health to re resent you at leant as well as von have been represented latttly I would never have offered myself to he your mem- ber. (Applause.) I have reason, the greatest reason, to thank God for the measure of health and strength that he gives me. (Applause.) I have every reason to believe that if my health is continued lam not-too old to represent you, my old friends, and I believe that at present you have no occasion to utter the words:—

div.head: CANDIDATURE OF SIR RICHARD CROSS.
div.p: THE CANDIDATURE OF SIR RICHARD CROSS.
MEETING AT ST. HELENS.

On Tuerday evening. Sir Richard Cross, the Conserve. l tive candidate for the Newton Division, addressed a large gathering of electors in the Drill Hall, St. Helens. Mr. W. Pilkington, of Roby Hall, presided ; apd amongst the 1 gentlemen on the platform were Mr. H. Seton-Karr, Con- servative candidate for St. Helenseand Mr. T. B. Royden, Liverpool.—The Chairman, after speaking of the services , of Sir Richard Cross, called for three cheers for the Home Secretary end Colonel Ireland Blackburue, for their services to South-West Lancishire.—Sir Richard Crots, who was receiver, with loud cheers, said he had to address them in three capacities. First, he had to thank them for the sup- port the electors of South-West Lancashire bad given to him SiRCE) 1855; and secondly, to the electors of the new I boroug,h of St. Helens he had to offer his hearty congratu- lations that they had attrained what they were so eminently entitled to—namely, a voice in the next Parlionient. He had also to address a word or two to anothor part of his audience, who were the constituents of the new Newton Division. hey had to decide between two principles, and they would have to answer for themselves and their con- sciences and to their children and those who came after them as to 'how they wished England to be governed in the future. He believed that the Midlothian promises were never fulfilled, and expectationa held out that bad never been reached. If Mr. Gladstone was stronger on one ques- tion than another it was the question of finance. The Con- I servativi expenditure in one year, he admitted, reached eighty-two and a half millions. But it would be found by comparison that the expenditure of Mr. Gladstone's Government had been a hundred mil- lions; and what had they for it ? Nothing. Yea, they had something : they had oceans of blood caused by the slaughter of thonkands of Arabs, whom they called " rebels," but who had really never rebelled against the English. ("Shame.") In regard to the depression of I trade, he asked if their expectations had 'been' fulfilled ? (" Nu ") Were profits larger to, manufacturers, were wages greater to workmen, end were they in a better pesition than before? ("No, no.") Referring to the appointment of the commission to inetaire into the depression of trade, Sir Richard said the Liberals were afraid to assist in it ; and on the question of Free Trade, he said he had always been a Free Trader, but he considered Free Trade ought to ho free on all sides. (A pplau4e.)—Mr. Alfred Wal meslay, Mr. Seton-Karr, Mr. Frederick Faram, Mr. I'. B. Boyden, and other gentlemen addressed the meeting, and a vote of cm- Science in the candidate was cirried, with few dissentients. MEETING AT RAINHILL. A meeting of the supporters of Sir Richard Grose was held in the National school, Rainbill, on Wednesday even- ingoehen tkere was a large attendance. The chair wee occupied by Mr. J. Birchall, who was supported by Mr. M. B. Westhead (Newton), Air. H. Hall, Government inspector of mines; Mr. W. H. Brook (Warrington), Mr. W. L. Evans, J.P. (Prescot), and other gentlemen. The, proceedings throughout were very enthusiastic. The Chairman alluded to Sir Richard Cross as being known to all the world as the best Home Secretary the present generation had seen. (Ap- plause.) Sir Richard A. Cross urged that it was the Con- servatives who gave the electors their proper share of repre- sentation by refusing to pass the Franchise Bill withoet the Redistribution of Seats. He said none of the Liberal speakers attempted to defend the action of the late Govern• resent during the last five years, but he would ask the people of England to say that the Government had done wrong, and had disgraced the coun- try. (Appleuse.) He accused them of having lowered the power of England in South Africa, and allowed the flag .of

(Applause.) Well, now, there is another question, and it is a question that has to be settled and decided by you working-men. My mind had been made up. It always takes two to matte a quarrel, and it often takes two to make an amicable settlement. I talked the matter over with, as I suppose you call toe lady at home, I talked the matter ever with my master. (Laugh- ter.) We came to the conclusion, she seemed to rather come to the conclusion that she would rather prefer to have my society, and we came to the conclusion that I should not stand again for the borough of Warrington. Well, that was our decision. That was settled. That was communicated to other gentlemen and to the party. But many and many a time in the street—l do not think I exaggerate if I say hendeeds of times—men have met me in the street and said "We hope you will fight again. We hope to return you. , again as our member." (Applause.) In addition to these outside kind feelings, for they were very kind feelings, I had 1 various deputations, working men in numbers, and more than one or more than two, who came and almost entreated me to stand again. Ido not think I yielded at the first,.but it ended in my saying "If von working men desire me to stand, if you'working men assure me that you have no other candidate who will stand, and if you tell me von are not likely to obtain a better candidate than myself, and if you tell me that you wish me to stand, remem- ber I am standing on , your account." And I stand upon the side of the working men now. That was wieat brought me before you as a Candidate for the thorough. (Applause) Well, L should have made a capital policeman. I know faces, and 1 have no doubt I shall see several Of your faces frequently. We are going to have various meetings, and I shall speak .to you, I I) ,in the same rational and simple manner in which I am now speak- ing, and subjects which are lert out to-night will be spoken of then. But I way to express what is the ruling, domi- nant thought in my mind at present. It is the question of trade. (Hear, bear.) Now, I think it is the beunden duty of every man in these hard times to see and to inquire what he tan do hitneelf in the direction of amending and improve trade. There is a Commission DOW which the late Govern- ment did everything they could to strangle. That commis- sion or committee is sitting. I hope it is investigating thoroughly and taking such evidence as will enable us to see some of the difficulties that there are in tr vie. Perhaps they may not be able to devise a cure, to t'n at we shill get outof all our troubles and all our difficulties, bat they may make some suggestions which will be for the good and the welfare of this country. (Applause.) Now, let us stand by that commission or committee. Let them take the oppor- tunity of making the fullest inquiry, and,let them state as fully as possible, and lay before the country the evidence they take and their report they make upon that evidence. Now, some people say that the proceedings of that commit- tee are to destroy Free Trade. Now, if that be tie case I should not say one word in its defenc:. lam a Free Trader, (Hear, hear.) I have been a Free Trader. I afil ready to say that great benefit has come to this country from the Itetion of Free Trade. But let us have a fair Inquiry, Let , A .1f Lilt

I*. C..Ma gERCY, who was receieed With cheers, said that lie would mention ins or two points that he thought the peoPie had a rtlat to insist upon from the new,Eadical,parti.' In the first place, tee thought some reforms Were necessary to make political representation abything like perfect in this country. They required an extension ote t,he powers of local government, and a system rabolistred which compelled:the spending in London of so roughenoney toyer enterprises like the ship canal. (Ap- plause.) He desired an arrangement whereby half of the money could be saved, and an investigation take place on the spot. He was also in favour of the one man one .vetel system. He wished that the Sovereign and the Prince of. Wales should be maintained in proper dignity, but protes- ted, in the name of millions of starving people, against there being maintained out of the public fund of England all the tribes of Hesse and Battenberg. The miners' programme asked for an inquiry into mine royalties, and he had some- thing to say on that subj,ct. He contended that whereas in %gland mine royalties to the extent of 6d per ton were paid whether or no a profit Was realised, in other countries no royalty was paid unless a profit had been realised. He I urged that it was unfair for a large royalty rent to have- to be paid, even therigh the mine in respect to which it was paid was ant worked at all. One firm in, Wigan had, alone. paid £260,000 for coal that had never, been worked by them. tine could England compete with France, Belgium, or Get- many with the iron and coal industries When Edgliale menu- factarers were placed at such a" dieadvaritage ? 'The miners of England asked for a Parliamentary inquiry into the operation of these Ti" al ties,ae compered with the operatien of eoyalties abroad. He believed that a revision of these royalties ' would at on63—iniproire the coil and iron trades of, tie country. (Applause-) -For his reart,, he did not wiah to rob a. landowner of one inch of his land, or a mineowner or one.ouoce of his coal, 'opt,* pee same tarne,hirthonght. that the benefit, God bed given _to a nation should be used Mit' for the iejary, but for 'the benefit of that nation. (Ape. platree,) He thought that the landowners Of England should be seeognised.simPly as trustees for the land, which they should use for the benefit of the people. They had it on the ,highest autlaoity that 500 millions of money could .be inveetid in the land of England, 'which, would make it captlile, of doubling its present pioduction. If that money was invested it would, find employment for— thousands now out of em-'' plovment, and find work for those who now over-crowded.' the towns. They required a reform of the land laws. The' new Radical party would, he thought, be sufficient to laei the foundation of a system of legislation' under which, 'be. fore many years had pa?sed, the labour markets would not Ile over-crowded; 'but there Would be plenty of work for all, and an era of prosperity would commence. (Ap- plause-)

Mr. oROSFIELD, who wan again received with cheers, said that questions had been banded to him, which he pro= cee;ded to answer. The first questipn was "A rumour it be. ing circulated iu,tbe town that Mr. WiltiamCro.fidd is con- nected with 'a firm, yrhich 'employs German workpeople in prefereAce to English on the ground that German labou• is cheaper than English; will Mr. Crosfield say whether that is true or not?" That he *as cstinected with a firm that employed German *or:Teeple was true, but that they em- ployed German workpeoole in preference to-English was Rot true : He was exceedingly 'glad that the question had been asked him. He had heard whispers, .but there was great difficulty in answering whistlers, for it was not always safe to trust to them. The firm with which he was counected commenced) MS zeicisrenc.) thirty veal age with the establishment of a sugar 213th:ivy. Sugar refining was then entirelv,in the hands of the Germans. Then it NY us a business of a highly technical character, in the bands of the Germans, and the establishment of such a business re- linirecrthe eniploerrieut of German men. There were 9thl in the employment of the firm men who cline into the em- ploy when first it was established in 1854. (Hear, hear.) The technical character of tho trade was passed, and it could now be carried on by English workmen, but he asked them as, fair and honest men whether it would be I right to put aside the faithful savants who had been em• ployed by the firm for thirty years, simply because they were Germatis, and replace them with Englishmen. (Cries of "No," and applause.) They hid been gooc; servants, and their masters wore as faithful to them as they were to their masters. (Applause.) In the list of the firm's em- ployees were a large number of German young men, re- presenting very many more than the men who originally came into the employ thirty years ago, who very largely consisted of the sons of those who were employed in the first instance by the firm. He thought that was a fair way of dealing with the Eng- lish born sons of German parents. (Applause.) "On the gronnci that German labour was cheaper than English" was not true. He would ask them, working men of Warringtop„ if they were prepared to carry out the principle which was suggested and isivolved in that question, that England should be made a little garden walled round, to the exclu- sion of skilled workmen from othe• countries. He thought they' were not. He would also point out that it involved the exclusion of masters of German birth as well as work. men, and he would ask them if they were prepared to advo- cate a principle of that kind—which would exclude such men a. Mr. Bulckow and Sir William Siemen. In the alkali trade did they think it would be ao 'advantage or a disad- vantage to. he rid ef the presence Of such men as Mr. Mond, or In the northern country would they like t see the works of Mr. Thewlison shut because he was a Getman? He thought that Cher would see that this was a two-sided ques- tion, and that Free Trade in labour—which was a thing he was glad to see that the Trades' Union Cenf,erences had gone in for recently—was a desirable thing. With regard to labour, it was very difficult to say what was cheap and what was dear. He had already told them that German labour was not cheaper than English, but he gathered from what he heard that the rumour was set about by his opponents. and he now made a challenge that an independent arbitraa tor should have access to the wages list of the firm with which he was connected, if the three firms he was about to mention, in Warrington, would grant the like access, so that a comparison might be made—Messrs. Stubs, Longford Wire Works, and Wilderspool Brewery. (Laughter and applause.) The second question given him was, "Is it true that after the Phoenix Park murders Messrs. Crosfield and Company discharged all or any of their Irish workpeople ? " The Phoenix Park murders occurred a long time in the past, and therefore he did not wish his answer to be supposed to cover all that time. If he understood the meaning of that question] he gave the answer in An emphatic no. (Applause.) The third question was, 9 Will you, if elected, vote for the repeal , of the compulsory Vaccination Acts ?" Here 1.6 could not I be quite so conciliatory as with regard to the other two questions. He could not consent off-hand to say that he would vote for that. He was a believer in the principle that I inoculation was a necessary safeguard to protect the popu- lation of England from a most grievous scourge. He wee prepared to believe that the way in which the Acts were car- ried out was not as perfect as might be, and he thouett that it was a subject for very grave inquiry as to how more pure matter could be supplied for the carrying out of the, Acts, which, he thought; must for a considerable time remain compulsory . He would go further into the question on other occasions, hut that was the answer he desired to give at present. (Applause.) Mr. Wretorrr said that he was the person who had asked the first question, which had been 80 satisfactorily answered l?y• their candidate. ,He then referred in denunciatory terms to false rumours circulated in the locality by a Tory print.

Mr. Jamas 'Rvaets proposed "That this meeting of the North-Wet Ward elecmrs pledges itself to use every legi- timate effort to secure ,the return of. Mr. William Cros- field, J.P. at the ensuing Parliamentary election by a Urge a:equity!' He was, be said, one of the happy individuals who were at the Tory meeting that had been referred t6—at the Lou Hotel--and he heard some of the speeches made The way in which each speaker looked towards the door in expectation of the arrival of Sir Richard Cross, reminded him .of a. story An connection with the.. Duke of Wellington. When the, Deke of Wellington was on the field of Waterloo bewail. eaid to have W ished that "night or Blucher would come." He observed at the meeting that the oratory was feeble, and that those who were appointed to speak had nothing to say. (Laughter.)' The Tories had no programme to present. The Liberal party had a pro- gramme, and, he believed, Mr. Crosgeld was one of those men who had not only an opinion oi ,his own, but who had the courage to maintaie. it, either Inside or outside the House of Cominons. (Applahee ) If they intended to win the election they rnust%work. (A Voice : "That's it, work and not talk") tie believed that they must not only work, but talk, too. I Leughtee.) Mr. LAWRENCE liVram seconded the resolution. He had no doubt that many of them lead read the ,address of Mr. .Crosfield, which he believed had giveh general satisfaction throughout the whole Liberal community.. There was not a Liberal in the torough who was not acquainted with the qualifications' of the candidate, and Milled no hesitation in saying that they eeiuld at all times depend upon him to support any measure that wOuld fend to the interest of the people. (Applause.) Mr. Crosfield, they knew, was a friend to the Irish, and he thought the Irish would be willing to support a man who had their intereets at heart. seeing that they had a. good candidate and a very weak Opponent, be thought that there . would be no difficulty, when the lime came, in returning Mr..Crosfi-kl, if they worked with the ces,fav;

div.p: what ran be said. Some people will nay thih cci -I put a tax upon corn again- am not with • do. I would never tolerate the slightest im- ehe food of the people of this country. You may as true, and that I mean it. You may take it as have long left it. You may see the ad- of an old man. (Laughter) In looking about my jnit before I same here, I found the copy of an 'which I pnblished to the electors of Warrington in .be yearlBs2. Now, I have told you what I think about a, tax upon-cern now. Would you like to know what I thostetil about a tax upon corn then in the year 1852. 1- have noe changed: In the year 1852 I said, "On the great question , of the day, the corn law, my mind, after the =tare delib- oration which the importance of the subject demanded, is, decided." Well, you want to know what it is. " I shall strengly oppose any re-imposition of duty upon corn." There is another subject. lam fer giving upon he best, the most liberal, the most charitable, and the most honour- able terms, education to all. He said a word about edncation I in those days, and he has not changed. "Education based on religion is one of the great bulwarks of social happiness andl prosperity, and F have always given it warm and zealous I support. I instine to the opinion that it will best be pro- moted by a more liberal grant from the public purse,, not by taxes," to carry cut that object. I Hope lam not making you feel as though you wanted your nightcape— (applause)—but there is ea subject which may well be men- tioned. Have you ever heard of such a thing as the Ship Canal ? (Applause.) Do you think we should all club to- gether as far as means go to support that project ? Don't you think we ought to have the work which the Ship Canal will require?' If we can get these works executed in this neighbourhood he would be a very foolish fellow who did not help with the purpese of bringing the'promoters of ' the Ship Canal to execute that work In this neighaourhoodal I have,never had any. hostility to the Ship Canal from the first. I always intended, when the Bill had passed, andt when the time came, I always considered it was my duty to give it a helping hand.. That helping hand I have given it, and lam very glad to-see that the best and oldest friend in the world I have, Lord Winmarleigh, has done the same. Did I subscribe my money to it with the view of making a profit? Perhaps you will think me a keen chap, but lam not 30 keen as that. I subscribed to the work of the Ship Canal simply and entirely because I think the proj -et is a good one for this neighboterhood—(epplause)—and to me the profit that I make upon the Ship Canal is as nothing compared to the benefit r think I am bringing to the in- habitants of this town—(hear, hear)—by joining the pro- moters in this execution/ Well, that is the reason I subscribed to the Ship Canal. There are a lot more snbjects I should like to speak upon, but I think it is much more wise to defer them to another evening, especially as my friend Mr. Pierpoint- will say something to you. In everything in this world a seneible man has an eye to busi- ness. Now, what is the main business that interests us upon this occasion? It is that we, the Conservative party in Warrington, who do acteuprightly, who mean to act up- rightly, who desire a good and a just Government, who desire to maintain the interests of our country, who desire to maintain our Church, add who desire to see our Church more and more diligent and-more and more active than it has been; who desire to see the Word of God properly taught, the duty that we owe to our Maker and the duties that we owe to each other properly laid before us, and laid before us in such a manner that we shall lay them to heart, and feel that we are in rise family desiring the glory of our God, and above all things after that desiring the well era of our fellow creatures. Well new, gentlemen, I have touched upon 90018 subjects, but I have a good deal more to say to you. I shall know you again. I hope we shall meet. fre• quently, and I hope you will be victorious. I hope, if I have the honour and the advantage of being your selected men, that nothing will be wanting in each of you, and in all of you together, to secure the desires of your hearts and the desire of my ambition. (Applause.) A resolution expressing contidende in the policy of .the present Government was then passed, on the motion of Mr. H. Appleton, seconded by Mr. Taylor, and supported by Mr. Robert Pierpeint. A vote of thanks to the chairman brought the proceedings to a close.

The funeral started iron& , Th'lcliog about ten o'clock, the coffin being taken by road to 41.,,s'eale. There were four or five mourning coaches and —ut twice as many private carriages. No plumes were Used and the ordinary undertakers trappings were con. ;rti`ciaously absent. SHOCKING DBATHS.—Abrabam Smith, employed in the nightsoil department of the Nottingham Corporation, was killed on Tuesday moreing in a shocking manner. div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, OCTOBER 31, 1885.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, OCTOBER 31, 1885.

SIR GILBERT GREENALL has evidently 'rrived at that age when, as SHARESPERE Says, the chin is double and the wit is single. He is before the electors of Warring- ton as a candidate for their suffrages, and more witless stuff than that which forms the staple of his speeches it is impossible to Conceive. He told the audience at the demonstration last week in support of his candidature that "that was not an occasion upon which he could give expression to his Political feelings or political opinions, but he hoped to be before them on many occa- sions.' If that was not a suitable occasion, it may well be asked—" Will there ever be One?" He is always, as they say from the stage of the Penny Show, "just a-going to begin , " with the difference that Sir Gil..- Baler's performance never does begin. He is like the clown who promises the ring- master half-a-crown, and who, when that gentleman holds out his hand for it, exclaims "You shall have it, but not now!" This is Pretty good as a circus joke; but its counter- part is very poor as a piece of electioneering. It is the way of the Wilderspool Brewer to gash over everybody on the platform whose name he happens "to remember. He has always a "free tap" of this kind, notwith- standing the Corrupt Practices Act; there is' atgood deal of praise, but nothing in the ' 81;ape of solid pudding. Sir GILBERT pre- . ! tuted on Monday night at a meeting held at ' yaresbury in support of the Tory candidate for the Knutsford Division. and he got to Wishing over absent friends; he gushed over ' sultowsr, and he gushed over JONES, and he gushed over ROBINSON. Can we wonder that Ithe audience showed signs of impatience? fl a speech made at Warrington on Tuesday rcening, Sir GILBERT did attempt something 2!e an exposition of his views; but he showed mniself so lamentably ignorant when he was ot characteristicly absurd that it would have 4en far better if he had held his peace. 1 ventured to speak of the late Govern- '4• ent as having "dragged the trade of this , e,°llntry down to nothing," when it is notori- ' ,t".tts to all who are familiar with trade statis- its that the volume was larger during the k AnsrorrE Administration than it was ever Dnown to be in the history of the country. may be that the Brewers have done less osiness ; but, as that means less suffer- °• g, less immorality, and less crime, it cannot _",ie said to 'be a matter of regret. The depression, such as it is, 'which exists in some branches of trade will not be remedied by the ltoyal Commission, which the Tory candidate tells us "the late Government had done every- thing they could to strangle." Our local .„h Rip van Winkle, like the HOME SE is "a little bit confusedCRETARY, I to be aware that the Royal does not seem not appointed until the presenotni Government was took office. Will somebody wake hiomvernmen pand tell him that it was impossible for "the, late' Government" to strangle that which did not exist. Sir GILBERT seems to have had it dinned into his ears that what is called Fair Trade won't do Carr it be that the word has been passed rotind that that card is played out ? The Tory candidate has apparently taken his cue from the Colonial Secretary, Who addressed his constituents at Preston on Saturday. Speaking in the Corn Exchange, Colonel STANLEY said.: "Knowing how im. kediately they were concerned with questions 21 trade, allow him to say one or two words, ttLe frankly avowed that be did not stand on tu:e same platform with Mr. ECROYD, whose v'ews on the question of Fair Trade he tnesPected, but did not participate in." Sir VLBERT GREENALL, delivering himself three afterwards, says "I have been a Free ;rader. lam a Free Trader. lam ready to 13Y that great benefit has come to this country vl'v'eln the action of Free Trade." And so the th4t4ogton Fair Trade bubble has burst, and trt_at, too, after special efforts—efforts the `lst ridiculous and fantastic—have been kacie to get it "in the air." We have always 4o !that it would not bear handling; it was °Ond to collapse when touched, for there , toWas _nothing in it. But what of the "Papers rthWorking-men" that were intended to make t; bubble seem beautiful in their eyes ? fikz3rhiAng the journal in which they were to be Nvllf:4 was always out of the question; and it th 'Lever do now for "the Club" even to give eto VABte a,way. Can nothing be done with "the d' • Well there is one way out of the lfrle 1 .2! utY • it's an ill wind that blows nobody hap:4, 4, Papers" will at least come in 13,e-rnY for the boys on the Fifth of Novem-

GmasnT, in his Election Address, and hl;4 EPe ech on Tuesday evening, indulges customary cant about having "the mi 11e,"°.,t! of the working classes deeply a •"' We wonder—to quote one of Lord 4ot ;I.l3l7ltY'S choice phrases—that the words " dke •e• choke him. He had their interests the ePIY at heart" when he bargained Ny!th at ,Orporation to get control of the fishing Work'? alton Reservoir, and then stopped as thinglY-rnen who sought to go fishing there_ lowece had done heretofore; when he al his agent to write to the Railway Coin-

pany with a view to closing the footpath to Morley Common ; and when he purchased the shooting rights over Aroley Meadows, not with the object of shooting there himself but in order to prevent working-men using a gun anywhere in the neighbourhood of Walton. No doubt all.this was very philanthropic ;but, unfortunately for the electoral prospects of the Tory candidate, the working-men of War- rington are not yet convinced that, when Sir GILBERT seems cruel, he is "cruel only to be kind." They do not forget that when he was previously in Parliament he was opposed to working-men in the country—his nearest neighbours having votes as had their brethren in the towns; and, whatever his feeling may be, they have it." very deeply at heart" that he voted in favour of flogging in the army! It is no use " rounding " on his friends, as he did on Tuesday even- ing, for the bribery and corruption in his interests, of which he admits they were guilty; he has himself to blame and not them for his defeat at the last election by the large majority of 529. He has been tried and found wanting; his record is a bad one ; and, if there is common sense in Warrington, his career, so far as Parliament is concerned, is closed.

COLONEL GAMBLE'S Address to the elec- tors of St. Helens will be found in our adver- tising columns. We observe that, like Mr E. K. MUSIPRATT, the Liberal candidate for the Widnes Division, he is in favour of Free Education ; he has evidently studied the subject in all its aspects, and does not, therefore, fall into errors which cause Tory politicians to stumble. He is convinced that it will not interfere with the teaching, as at present, of religion in denom- inational schools ; and, further, that it will put voluntary schools more on a footing of equality with Board Schools. He does not speak without authority. Addressing the electors of Parr on Tuesday, Col. GAMBLE said "he had taken every opportunity to speak to clergymen of all denominations, including some Catholic priests, and he knew that the opinion had changed very greatly within the last few days." It has been too readily taken for granted that Cardinal MANNING was opposed to freeing the schools; but his Eminence has at last set all doubts on the subject at rest. In the course of a sermon on Sunday last. at the pro- Cathedral, in London. lie said "he was not going to speak against free education, and there was no danger of Catholics being on the unpopular side in the matter." It will be seen, therefore' that Mr. SETON-KARR is likely to be left high and dry in his opposi- tion ; for we understand his own spiritual master--the Archbishop of CANTERBURY— takes the view held by Colonel GAMBLE on the education question. Surely when two high Church dignitaries like Cardinal MAN- r XING and the Archbishop of CANTERBURY have declared that they are not opposed to Free Education the rest of their followers may feel assured that there is no need for alarm. Colonel GAMBLE is right in saying that Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S proposal in the first instance ' took away people's breath ; but they are recovering themselves. It is beginning to ; be seen that the abolition of the fees leaves the schools, the children and re- ligious instruction .untouched. Lord RAN- DOLPH CHURCHILL talks of a Penny Fee as a compromise; but this is playing at "chuck-farthing" with the question. How pleasant to think of poor parents having to undergo the humiliation of applications which they regard as pauperising, and all for the sake of a Penny Fee! Lord RANDounr, as the mouthpiece of the Conservatives, makes them look ridiculous. He has not always haggled in this way over the last copper. Speaking at Birmingham on the 17th of April, 1884., upon the occasion of laying the foundation stone of a new school, be said:

- I believe that the question of national education must shortly be dealt with by Parliament in a large and liberal spirit, and I believe that it is un- doubtedly connected with the great question of local taxation. I know of no method more appro- priate or more politic by which the local burden could be relieved than by the State taking upon itself the whole expense connected with the national education of the country. This will be done, I have no doubt, by following the lines of the Education Act of 1870, by the State availing itself of all the machinery which it finds at work and actually in existence for the purpose of promoting education, and by subsidizing that machinery, whatever may be its nature, to the extent of the expense they may have incurred in the elementary education of each child. What is this, we would ask, but Free Educa- tion?

div.p: MR. J.E.BARLOW, the Liberal candidate for I the Knutsford Division of Cheshire, is mak- ing headway with the electors. He has ad- dressed various meetings—several during the past week—and has everywhere been most favourably received. He has issued a capital address, in which he treats of home and foreign affairs in a style which shows that he is familiar with these matters, and that he comes before the constituency with definite principles and lofty aims. With regard to foreign policy, he points to the success which Mr. GLADSTONE'S Government achieved in increasing the cordiality of feeling existing between the mother country and the colonies, and refers to the attachment shown to British rule by the people of India whilst Lord RIPON was Viceroy. He believes that a policy which has excited a feeling of this kind in the past is the one to pursue in the future in dealing not only with India and our colonial possessions, but with foreign countries. He is not blind, as some of the Tories are, to the failure of the Berlin Treaty, and quotes General GORDON'S statement that "the Treaty of Berlin did no good to Turkey but infinite harm to Europe." Mr. BARLoIv sees the need of various reforms in order that the farmer and his men may reap the full benefit of their labour on the land. To those who hesitate as to who is the "farmer's friend," he points out that, whilst it is impos- sible to produce any Act of real value which othe t hCeoangsriercyuaittiuyreasi have class,ave ptahs the eLd ibne rthe a ls can interests ccite as achievements an amended Agricultural Holdings Act, the Ground Game Act, and the ureepeeda,looffctuhuersMe, alftutxr further il e T legislation.p erce i perceives th bute would not be content with such a paltry fau change as Lord SALISBURY suggests in the proposal to register titles. He would do this and more; he would go to the root of the matter, abolish entail and %jinneniture and set the land free. And this is not. all ; Mr. BARtOW IS amongst those who believe , that farmers should have secured to them freedom of cultivation,and full compensation for unexhausted improvements. He thinks it hard that they should . be handicapped by railway companies charging high rates for the carriage of farm produce, and, if elected, he will do what he can to ensure that their grievance in this respect shall be remedied. Tithes, in his opinion, should be abolished,

seeing that they are " cne important cause of land falling out of cultivation in many districts." With regard to the housing of the poor, both in town and country, the Liberal candidate for Knutsford thinks there is great room for improvement; and he is amongst those who believe that we may have " free primary education without preju- dicially affecting denominational schools." From these leading articles of his political creed, it will be seen that the Liberalism of Mr. BARLOW is of a robust kind. The. electors of the Knutsford Divison will do themselves credit by returning him ; he is the right sort of man to represent an agricul- tural constituency.

FURIOUS DRIVING AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Pety See. stone, on Monday, Thomas Trayner, employed by Mr. E. Johnson, grocer, was charged with furious driving.—P.S. Wballey lasted that on Wednesday night. the 21st inst., the defendant was driving a horse and trap down Bridge. street at a gallop, and although cautioned by the officer, he continued the animal at its furious pace.—The defendant, who pleaded guilty, was fined 20s and c ,sts, On 60. At Runcorn Police Court, on Toursday, before Captain C. W. Haztehurst and Mr. A. Thomas, Christopher Con- nolley, 16 years' of age, who has served several years in a reformatory school, was charged with stealing a shirt worth 3s 6d, the property of Ann Wakefield. a widow residing in Albert-street. Ibe shirt was hanging on a line to dry. Prisoner had been in the neighbourhood selling shrimps, and he was caught in the act of pawning it with Mr. lmison. Church-street, by P.C. Breeze, who apprehended him.— He was sentenced to a month's hard labour. ALLEGED THEFT OF HAMS AT WlDNES.—Yeaterday at Widnes Police Court, before Mr. Holbrook Haskell, junr., Catherine Martin, and her son, Robert John Martin, 13 years of age, and Joseph Quinn, 11 ye as of age, were charged with stealing two hams, vain.. 225, from the shop of Mr. John Quinn, grocer and provision dealer, Gerrard' street, Simms Cross. The hams were missed from the yard of the shop on the previous evening, and about 10 o'clock P.C. Strickland searched the house of Martin, and hidden beneath a lot of rubbish feund the missing hams. Young Martin made a statement incriminating Quinn, who was also apprehended.—Remanded. UNLAWFULLY WOUNDING AT WlDNES.—Before Mr. Hol-

brook Gaskell, junior, at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, John Johnson was charged with unlawfully wounding Ann Siincock, wife of a marine store dealer, living in Appleton- street. On Saturday sight the 17th met, the prisoner . .

, I entered the shop and asked for some matches. Upon his request being refused, he spoke some most filthy language, and struck Mrs Simcock on the forehead jost above the eye with a brush handle. Mrs Simcock was felled to the ground by the force of the blow, and bled very much. The handle was smashed into three pieces—Dr. McCambridge, who had dressed the wound, said it was a dangerous one and might have been caused by such a wearin as that described.—The prisoner alleged that. Mrs Simcock struck him three times and he only retaliated. Her husband and be had had a fight and "of course" her husband got the worst of it. The prisoner was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial.

BONA FIDE TRAVELLERS DEFINED AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Police, on Monday, Mrs. Griffiths, landlady of the George Inn, Pool-lane, was summoned for keeping her (house open during prohibited hours. George Hill and John Hill, of Union-street, were charged with being upon the premises. Mr. A. Fletcher, of Nortbwich, defended. On Sunday night, the 4th inst., P.C.'s Hammersley and Breeze found the door of the George Inn partly open, and entered. In a back room Were four men besides the defendants' two sons. Mrs. Griffiths said they were all lodgers. Defend- ants, she said, were the nephews of Alexander Hemilton, a tailor, who had lodged with her for about five years.—Wit- nesses for the defence proved that on the Saturday afternoon Hamilton and his nephews went to Manchester to see the Ship Canal demonstration. They returned on Sunday night at half-past ten, and at the invitation of Hamilton they went to the George Inn for supper.—The Bench were of , opinion that these men, having travelled from Manchester, ' where they had slept, were hoiza fide travellers, and even if near home entitled to refreshment, as they might not have any in the house. The police were, however, quite justified in bringing forward the case, which would be dis- missed.

_ FELONIES AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, On Wednesday, Margaret Cassidav, a married woman, was charged with having on the 23rd September, stolen a sin- glet, value 3s 3d, from the shop of Mr. Frederick Tebbutt, draper, Ann-street. The prisoner made a small purchase in the shop, and on her departure the singlet was missed. She , afterwards attempted to pawn the article. Pleading guilty' the prisoner was fined 10e.—Margaret Redmond, a married woman, was charged with stealing a shawl from the person of Frances Brown of 44, Walre;y-Street. The women on Saturday night had a slight disturbance. The prisoner snatched the shawl from Mrs. Brown's shoulders, and it was afterwards found partially burnt away in front of the prisoner's house. When apprehended by P.C. Bruce the prisoner was drunk, and said she did not remember any- thing about it.—Mr. J. W. Knowles, who defended, sub- mitted there was no case of felony against the prisoner, who was much provoked by the prosecatrix. The case was dismissed, but the prisoner bad to pay Sc and the value of the shawl, in order to stay further proceedings,—Wilfred Jen- nion, a young man, was charged with having on Saturday night stolen three bens, value 9e., the property of Rh hard Lucas, farmer, Norlands-lane, Widnes. The prisoner was remanded for a week —itargaret Esmond, 17, and Mary Jane Doyle, 16, pleaded guilty to stealing a bed tick worth is, the property of Francis Byrne, labourer, of 8. Vine- street. Whines. Esmond, who bad been previously con- victed, was sent to gaol for a month, and Doyle was sen- tenced to a fortnight's hard labour.—John Butler, 14,1 William Tarleton, 14, and Joseph Tarleton. 12, were charged , with having, between 230 on Saturday, the 24th, and 6.30 1 a.m. on Monday, the 26th inst., broken into a hut in Moor- lane, belonging to the Local Board, and stolen a jacket, three bags, one saucepan, and other articles. worth 10s, the ' property of Thomas Hatton, labourer, Warringten-road. Butler and William Tarleton sold many of the articles to Mr. Simcock, marine store dealer, Appleton.street, and one of the stolen articles was found in Butler's home. The younger Tarleton FM discharged; his bother, who had been previously convicted, was committed to gaol for 14 days, and then to go to a reformatory school fir four years. Butler was sentenced to receive twelve strokes with a birch rod. THE ELECTION IN NEWTON DIVISION.—There is every reason to believe that the election in the Newton Division of South-West 'Lancashire will I take place during the first week in December. Messrs. Welsby, Hill, and Smallshaw, Parliamentary agents of the Sheriff of Lancashire, will attend at the Newton Town Hall during the week commenc- ing the 23rd November for the purpose of receiving nominations of candidates, and, it is stated, the votes given for the respective candidates will be counted at the Town hail on the sth December. REDUCTION OF RAILWAY RATES. We are in- , formed that the Lancashire and Yorkshire and the London and North-Western Railway Companies have resolved upon a revised list of rates for the carriage of goods between Manchester and Liver- pool, and that the other railway companies are likely to take the same course, if, indeed, they have not already decided upon it. It is estimated by the companies that there will be a saving to traders of not less than from 5 to 10 per cent upon the present charges. The Cheshire Lines Committee have announced a reduction in the rates for bale goods, cotton, timber, grain, and other articles, be- tween Liverpool and a number of Lancashire and Cheshire stations, commencing on the 2nd prov. DR. MecilrE's CANDIDATURE AT MONTROSE.— The Montrose Beview says —ln the Montrose Burghs, Dr. Mackie goes on his way rejoicing, cheered by the too sanguine expectations and, in- deed, absurd anticipations of some of his supporters, who by a method of calculation, unknown at least to Liberals, actually talk of his chances of success. With so many grave and important questions before the country it is certainly astonishing to find that Dr. Mackie has so little to say on practical politics. We admit that he is pursuing his candidature with a considerable degree of good humour, notwith- standing a great deal of self-assertion and self- laudation. His speeches, however, if relieved of the interpolations would be sorry reading, and would certainly impart little instruction or political enlightenment. There is really little to criticise in his political effusions. They partake too much of the character of long and tedious introductions, a never- ending pouring forth of words, with scarce a grain of political wisdom. The candidate in fact is well defined in the blunt and out-spoken words of one of his audience on Friday night—an "empty bubble." DATE OF THE ELECTIONS.—It is announced that Parliament will be dissolved on Wednesday, Nov. 18th. If the precedent of 1868—the last dissolution that took place during the recess—be followed, the new writs will be issued on the same day, and will be received by the returning officers on the follow- ing morning in most parts of England and Wales. Assuming that the writ has been received by the returning officer on November 19th, the possible times for nomination and poll in boroughs are as follow : Nov., Wednesday, 18th, dissolution ; Thursday, 19th, receipt of writ; Friday, 20th, last possible day for notice of election ; Monday, 23rd, first possible day for nomination; Tuesday, 24th, last possible day for nomination; first possible day for poll ; Thursday, 26th, last possible day for poll. In counties the corresponding dates, assuming again that the writ is received on the 19th, would be as fol- low:—Nov., Thursday 19th, receipt of writ; Saturday 21st, last day for notice; Monday 23rd, earliest day for nomination; Tuesday 24th, earliest day for nolling. Dec., Tuesday Ist, earliest day for nom- ination; Monday 7th, earliest day for polling. The Daily News says :—Much controversy exists as to whether the neNt Parliament will be summoned this year. A consideration of the circumstances shows that such a proceeding is literally impossible With the dissolution taking place on the 18th of Novem- ber, and taking into account the necessity of an in- terval of thirty-five days between the dissolution and the meeting of a new Parliament, it would not .be competent for the new Parliament to meet be- fore the 23rd of December, an encroachment upon Christmas-time thatis not likely to be contempla- ted. Some ipis-apprehension has arisen from the fact that the Parliament elected in 1868 met twenty- eight days after the dissolution. But that was an exceptional case especially legislated for, and does not affect the general rule.
