THE LATE MR. NORMAN, OP RUNCORN. On Tuesday night a general meeting of the committee of the Runcorn Young Men's Christian Society was held in the reading-room, High-street. Mr. John Johnson presided. Mr. S. C. Beckett, as one of the oldest members of the asso- ciation, moved that a vote of condolence be passed to the members of the family of the late president of the associa- tion, Mr. Thomas Norman. They mourned one who stood at the head of that AssJciation, and one who had always taken the &epee interest in its welfare. If there was one thing which perhaps relieved their sorrow it was that Mr. Norman died a happy death, and that some of his last ac- tions were truly in keeping with a Christian character. As the members of a Christian association they rejoiced in the fact, believing that no friend could die with a better hope than that be was going to a better world, where there should be no cares, and where everything was joy and peace. Captain Le C mrteur seconded the proposition. Day after day little episodes were brought to light which revealed the noble and generous character of Mr. Norman. They all knew that Mr. Norman had sprung from the ranks to an honourable position in the town ; but they could all testify to the fact that his pride had not increased, and that to the end he was the same humble Themes Norman they knew 30 years age.—Mr. W. Pownall (secretary) supported the , motion, observing that Mr. Norman had always done his utmost to promote the prosperity of the association, and to give assistance to those around him. Just before his death he requested that £5 should be given towards the gymnasium, and his kindness and forethought were shown I by the fact that a short time prior to his death he sub- I scribed half a cuinea towards the aged persons' t-eat which would tilts place in January.—The Chairman, in putting I the resolution to the meeting, said Mr. Norman's loss he I -personally felt very deeply indeed; and his loss to the town and to that association in particular was very great.—The motion was carried unanimously.—On the motion of Mr. William Shaw, seconded by Mr. Meredeth, Mr. Beckett, the ex-president, was appointed to fill the vacant presidency.
WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONS, RUNCORN.

The annual sermons in aid of the Wesleyan Home and. Foreign Missions were preached in Runcorn on Sunday. At St. Paul's Chapel the Rev. James Crabtree, of Manches- ter, occupied the pulpit both morainv and evening. In the I morning Mr. J. Parker preached at Camden School Chapel, and in the evening the Rev. George Wood, the superinten- dent minister, delivered a sermon at the earns place of wor- ship. There were good congregations at both chapels. A meeting of the juvenile branch of the missionary society I was held in Brunewick School on Sunday afternoon, and the proceedings were of a very encouraging character. Mr. John Simpson presided and delivered an address. Addresses were also delivered by Messrs. D. Bisbrown and B. Kniveton. The total amount collected and subscribed in the school was £77 15s.

On Monday evening the annual missionary meeting was , held in St. Paul's Chapel. There was a good congregation. ' Mr. R. Shaw presidel, and he was supported by the Revs. James Crabtree, William Wilson (late missionary in Fiji), the deputation, George Wood, T. Hackett and W. Vause (Free Church), A. P. Watson; Messrs. John Simpson, T. Simister, B. Kniyeton, and E. Taylor. The Rey. W. VallBo offered up prayer. Mr. T. Simister read the report. The income of the society for 1884 amounted to £146,308 Os 44, and the ex- penditnre £146,289 15s id, leaving a surplus of £lB 4s 6d. The contributions from Runcorn for 1885 were as follows: —Collected by Mrs Soulbv, sa Os 64; Miss Harrison, £5 ' 18s 63; Miss Norman and Miss Peacock, £l4 12s; Miss Simister, £8 14s; Mr and Mrs Johnson's box, 15s; public , collections on .the previous day: St. Paul's, £l5 15s 2d ; !Camden School Chapel, £l. At Camden School the male class had contributed £5 3s 4,1; female class, £3 8s 10d; !girls, £l7 lOs 4d ; boys, £2 3s 10d; infant class, .5s ; ' collected on the previous day, 108 6d ; total, £29 2s; an increase of £9 12s 7.1 on the previous year. (Applause.) St. Paul's School : ' Subscribed by girls, £3 lie 44 ; subscribed by boys, £6 12s 81; boys with books, £2O 1.4 s 74 ; girls with books, £23 44 7d ; public collections in school, £1.2 6s 103 ; total £77 158 54; an increase of £ll lOs Bd. (Applause.) The total amount received up to that sight, including the previous day's collections was £162 124 7d, being an increase of £lB 16s 3d. (Applause.) The Chairman, in a brief speech, expressed his pleasure at being present in that position that evening, lie believed the way in which the young people in conuection with their Sunday Schools had entered into this missionary work was one of the chief causes of the very high position in which Runcorn stood with reference to missionary work. The Sunday echoel officers had solved the secret of success by getting the young people to engage heartily in the work. (Hear, bear.) If their young people commenced they would never leave off these works and deeds of good- UM. (Hear, hear.) He made a touching reference to the late Mr. Norman. The Rev. James Crabtree spoke of the influence and power of the Bible, and said let' no one fear that in the ad- vance of science and the match of intellect, Jesus Christ would be left behind; that men would outgrow Him, as they had outgrown the philosophy and science of the past. Jesus Christ was contemporary with all age. (Hear, hear.) The diffusion of Christian Church and Christian knowledge dur- ing the last 70 or 80 yeort vas a most remarkable phenome- , non of this, which Max Milner called, a " momentous Icentury." (Applause.) He pointed out the progress made 'amongst the Hindoos and other Indian nations during the past half-century.—The Rev. William Wilson delivered an interestiag speech upoe his labours in Fiji, and the admira-• ble results that had accrued from the missionary enterprise thero.—The Rev. G. Wood moved, and the Rey. A. P. Vi'atsoa seconded, a vote of thanks to the deputation, which was carried with acclamation.—On the proposition of Mr. B Kniveton, a vote of thanks was accorded to the committee ace' the collectors for their services daring the past year.— Mr. John Simpson moved, and Mr. Simister seconded, a vote of thanks to the chairman, which was carried, and the pro- ceedings terminated.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY:
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY:

_ The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Lieutenant-Colonel Ashton presided, and there were present the Revs .1 Lockwood, J W N Tannet, Messrs Hadfield, Wallington, W Whitlow, Stokes, Lewis, Parr, Aaron, Percival, Linaker (clerk), Wli Linaker (deputy clerk), and J Farrington (nuisance inspector).

div.head: THE-INCIDENCE OF TAXATION.
div.p: THE-INCIDENCE OF TAXATION.

' A discussion took place on the incidence of local taxa- tion, and complaints were made by Mr W Whitlow, Mr Parr, and Mr. Stokes. of the increase Is the sanitary rate for the current half year upon the previous year. It was stated it was nearly double the previous calls.—The Deputy Clerk said the rate was increased in order to give the Authority a working balance. They had had from time to time to go to the treasurer, and there had been some un- pleasant correspondence about the overdraft.—The Chair- man suggested that a committee should be appointed to consider the income of the sanitary rate.—Mr Whitlow said it would be much better if the landlord paid these rates, and things that were for the benefit of his property and land, and then the tenant farmer would know what he had really to pay.—Mr Aaron said he had questioned Mr Verdi, 'Con- eervative candidate for liorthwich 'Division, if he would cots for an alteration in the incidence of taxation, and be had replied that he would not.—Mr Hadfield: Put it to Mr Brunner, the Liberal candidate, then.—Mr Aaron: He will promise anything, will Mr Brunner.—Mr Parr: He's as bad as Mr Chamberlain.—The Deputy Clerk said it was no use asking Mr Brunner or Mr Verdin. The best plan would be to write to the Presi- dent of the Local Government Board, and the late President. and ask them if they would bring into Parliament a measure to put taxation on a fair basis.— On the proposition of Mr. Stokes, seconded by Mr. Aaron, a committee, consisting of the chairman, Meagre. Weir, Parr, Stokes, and Mclntyre was appointed tn ascertain the cause of the increase in the sanitary rate, and to consider the advisability of communicating with the pregnant and late president ef the Local Government Board with regard to the unjust incidence of local taxation. FRODSHAM PAROCHIAL COMMIITRE. At the meeting of this Committee on Friday, Mr. A. Thomas, J.P.' in the chair, the question of a ventilating shaft for the Overton sewer was submitted for final con- sideration and in the absence of any further communica- tion from Mr. Edmonds in reference to an alternative proposal. it was resolved that the engineer be instructed to have the ventilating lamp pillar erected in the place Indicated by the Cmimittee. It was reported that the excavation for flushing chamber in connection with Overton drainage had taken the wati.r from the public well, and it was decided that a tender be obtained to deepen and im prove the well, and to endeavour to recover the supply of water.

div.head: FROBSITAM.
div.p: FROBSITAM.

_ RIFLE VOLUNTEERS.—The annual distribution of prizes took place in the Town Hall last evening. Under pressers on our space, we hold over our report. MISSIONARY SERMONS AND MESTING.—Special SeII:RODS were preached in the Trinity Chapel, Frodstiam, on Sunday, by Rev. J. H. Jones, of Warrington, on behalf of the Wes- leyan Foreign Missions. The annual meeting was held in the Same chapel on Monday evening, when the chair was taken by Mr. Samuel Okell. The Rev. Edwin Messcrop read the report, from which it appeared that the Frodsbam circuit had contributed upwards of £B4 to the funds of the society during the past pear. Addresses were given by the Chairrcan, Rev. J. H. Jones, and the Rev. John C. W. Gostick, who had been in the south of India for ten years as a missionary. The collecttons after the sermons and meeting amounted to £l4 12s 7P. BRODSRAM AND HELSBY DRAINAGE BOARD.—A. general meeting of ratepayers within the area of the ahove district was held at the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Tuesday evening, for the purpose of examining and settling the accounts of the Beard for the past year and selecting two auditors. The chair was taken by Mr. Thomas Davies, and there were also present Messrs. John Priestner, James Percival, William Booth, and Charles E. Linaker, clerk and survevor.—The Clerk to the Beard read the statement of account.; for year , ended 29th September, 1885, viz. :—Receipts: Balance, £4B 164 1l4; rate collected, £207 6s 84; interest, 3s 74; total, £256 7s ad. Expenditure: Cleaning out watercourses. Frodsham, £36 19e 44; Helsby, £l2 lie 6d; printing, audi• , tore' fees, and other general charges, £ll 9s 6d; Parliament tary expenses. re Ship Canal, £6B 4s 6d; legal expenses, I£3 4s 10d; salary of clerk and surveyor, £3O; balance, £93 17a 61d ; total, £256 7s 211. It was explained that the Shipp. 'Canal expenses had been paid by the landowners in almoir every case. It was decided to appoint one auditor instead of two as heretofore, and it was resolved that Mr. Abraham White, of Helsby, be appointed with a fee of 10s 6d for his services. Mr William Booth inquired what was inclutled 'in the charge for legal expenses, when the Clerk replied that the amount was incurred for legal assistance in advis- ing as to tbe powers of the Board to enforce payment of rates and settling forms for legal proceedings against de- faulters.—There was no objection to the accounts, and the meeting terminated.

RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting was held on Tuesday, Lieut.- Colonel Ashton presiding. Present—Rev. J. Lockwood, J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Weir, Lewis, Parr, Aaron, Stokes, Bagnley, Hadfield, Wallington, %V. Whitlow, Smith, Per- cival, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. IL Linaker (deputy clerk). THE LATH MR. THOMAS NORMAN.—The Chairman called the attention of the Board to the loss the Union had sus- tained in the death of Mr. Thomas Norman, who had for many years occupied a seat at the Board as one of the Guardians of Rnncorn. lie was punctual in his attend- ance, never shirked his duty—nay, he was always ready and willing to do more than he was called upon to do; and he felt sure the members would wish to put on record some token of their respect and regard. (Hear, hear.) He there- fore begged to propose " That this meeting expresses the deepest feelings of sorrow and regret at the death of Mr. Thomas Norman. They regard the event as a great loss not only to the Board, but to the poor of Runcorn, and they desire to express to his family their deep feelings of condo- lence at the loss they had sustained."—Mr. Weir (deputy chairman) seconded the resolution. Mr. Norman was a very good representative of the ratepayers, and a true guardian of the interests of the poor in his neighbourhood, and he was sure they were all deeoly sorry at his sudden death.— The motion was carried anatilmously.—On the motion of Mr. Aaron, seconded by Mr. Weir, Mr. Philip Speakman was appointed a member of the Assessment Committee in place of Mr. Norman. THE POLICE WANTED AT WESTON.—Tbe Deputy Clerk read the following letter from Col. J. H. framersley, chief BILLINGE AND WINSTANLEY FRIENDLY SOCIETY.—OR constable for Cheshire have the honour to , Monday a miscellaneous entertainment was given in Bit- acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 20th must, linge Parish Church schools by the members and friends of forwarding resolution of Board of Guardians of Runcorn the Billiuge and Winstanley Friendly Society, the proceeds Union, relative to alleged want of police protection at ,of which are to go towards purchasing a banner for the club. Weston ; and in reply have to inform the Board of Gnar- ' The Rev, Howard Si.. George, M.A., president, occupied the diens that the constable stationed at Weston was by my chair.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

MRS. CATHERINE JAMES, widow of the late Mr. Thomas Janos, proprietor of the Theatre Royal, Runcorn, died, after a lingering illness, at an early hour OD Wednesday morning. Loss or A RUNCORN SCHOONER.—The schooner A. M. Brundrit, of Runcorn, has been totally wrecked on Black Island, Newfoundland. The crew are saved. The vessel, which was not insured, was owned by several Runcorn gen- tlemen. DITTON BAND OF HOPE.—The first entertainment of the season was given by this society, assisted by friends from Widnes, in the Wesleyan Schoolroom, Ditton, on Wednesday evening last. The chair was taken by Mr. S. Reed, of Wid- nes. There was a good programme. RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—On Wednesday even- ing an engine went off the rails near the Widnes London and North-Western Railway Station. A few " chairs " were smashed and rails injured, and single line had to be worked for about two hours. SECOND RUNCORN STARR-BOWEETT BUILDING SOCIETY.— The first annual report has been issued. During the year 225 share certificates, representing 472 shares have been issued, and five appropriations have been made. There is a balance in the bank of £4OO. BETHESDA MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—On Wed- nesday, Mr. Thomas Lydiate read a paper on the subject of "The Authorship of the Pentateuch." Great interest was centred in the paper, judging from the large attendance and hearty discussion which followed the essay. Mr. Wyllie Presided. WESTON POINT WESLEYAN CHAPEL—The anniversary sermons were preached on Sunday by the Rev. A. P. Wat- son. As a token of respect to the Memory of the late Mr,' Thomas Norman. Handel's "Dead March" in Saul was played, and the choir sang "Vital spark." The chapel was draped in black. ART CeAss FOR RtnecoaN.—Mr. W. G. Knight, an artist who received his training at the Warrington,Art School, under Mr. Thompson, has commenced an art school at Run- corn, under a committee of local gentlemen, with Mr S Pope as secretary. The project is the outcome of the discussion at the Free Library Committee. GCOD TEMPLARISM AT WIDNES.—The following officers have been appointed to the Hope at Appleton Lodge 1.0. GT. :—W.C.T.. Bro. T. E. Hill; W.V.T.. Sister M. Corns; W.S., Bro. T. Harrison ; W.F.S., Bro. I. Corns ; W.T., Bro.. W. Hill; W.C.. Sister E. Hill, junr.: Bro. R. Leather : W.G., Bro. Salt; W.S.H., Sister T. Reay. GYMNASIUM FOR RUNCORN.—The committee of the Young Men's Christian Association have succeeded in arranging fora gymnasium to be formed in the town. Mr. A. Alexander, director of the Liverpool Young Men's Christian Association gymnasium, has been consulted, and this gentleman will have control of the arrangements. The institution is expected to be open in a few weeks. RTJNCORN AND THE GENERAL ELECTION.—The members of the Runcorn branch of the Irish National League have resolved to vote at the general election as Mr. Parnell and his party may direct. On Monday night the Salvation Army had a meeting, and deckled to throw in their lot with Mr. Brunner, principally because of his expressed opinions on the social purity question and the prosecution of Mr. Stead and his colleagues. ACCIDENT TO A BOY AT WIDNES.—Thomas Smith, six years of age, residing in Warrington-road, met with a seri- ous accident on Wednesday evening. With several other boys, he was playing with a gate belonging to Mr. Hewitt, grocer, Warrington-road, when the gate fell from its hinges upon him, and he sustained severe internal injuries. He was carried in an insensible condition to his home, where he was attended by Dr. McCambridge. His condition is re- garded as very dangerous. GALLANT RESCUE AT RUNCORN.—James Rebioson, a boatman on the flat "Frederick," performed a gallant deed on Thursday afternoon. A boy fell into the canal at Weston Point from a bat that was moored there. Robinson saw the occurrence, and although possessed only of one arm, plunged into the water, seized the drowning boy, and after great difficulty brought him to the side where they were both pulled on the bank. This is not the first time Robinson has saved life, and his bravery deserves recog- nition. THUNDERSTORM AT RUNCORN AND WIDNES.—A storm of vivid lightning and loud thunder peals, accompanied by rain and hailstorms of exceptional size, broke over these towns on Tuesday night. There was also a very high wind. No damage of a serious character was done. In Victoria-road, Widnes, the cellars of many tradesmen were flooded, as usual, and the receding waters have left a large quantity of sediment of a very disagreeable nature. The low-lying fields at Ditton presented the appearance of a lake, and the road near the post office was flooded. BETHESDA CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL, RUNCORN.—The Rev. J. D. Thomas, pastor of this place of worship, intro- duced a service of gn exceptional character on Sunday even- ing last. The need of a departure from old methods, if the masses are to be attracted to divine worship and retained amongst the congregation, is generally recognised, and the service in Bethesda Chapel on Sunday met with considerable Success. It was a" people's service." Every seat was free; a person entering the edifice was made heartily welcome, and allowed to study his own convenience and pleasure in taking his seat; and a fair congregation assembled. Sankey's hymns were used, a layman. Mr. Joseph Slade, offered up prayer, and the pastor preached an appropriate sermon, the preceedings being altogether on a popular ' basis. Mr. Ravenscroft presided at the organ. Similar services will be held at intervals during the whiter. PRESENTATION TO A RUNCORN EMPLOYER—Mr. Wm. Farrell, builder and contractor, South Bank. Runcorn, at- tained his 60th birthday on Sunday last, and on the pre- vious day his numerous workmen assembled at the house of Mr. W. R. Wase, Wellington Hotel, to celebrate the auspicious occasion. Mr. W. G. Cunningham presided over the proceedings. An illuminatad address and an electro- plated cruet stand were presented to Mr. Farrell by the men through Mr. John Dobson, the oldest employe, who ex- pressed the feelings of regard and respect in which Mr. Farrell was held. Tbe Chairman delivered a neat speech, and several workmen also spoke. Mr. Farrell briefly acknowledged the gift. The testimonial reads as follows : " This testimonial is presented to Mr. W. Farrell, builder, South Bank, Runcorn, by the workmen employed by him, as a token of their great respect and hi,gh estimation of his business talent, industry, and enterprise, and as a commem- tnoration of his attainment of his 60th birthday, and to express the hope that he may live to see many happy returns in health, wealth, and prosperity. October 25th, 1885." CARDINAL MANNING ON FREE EDUCATION. Cardinal Manning preached at the pro-Cathedral, Kensington, on Monday, on Christian education. He said this country was upon an inclined plane, and though the descent might be slow it would be sure unless it was arrested. The School Board sys- tem was essentially unjust ad well as dangerous, be- cause it threw all the power into the hands of secu- larists, and gave them command of almost a limit- less revenue from the rates. He was in favour of universal education for the poor, and in his diocese 20 per cent, of the Catholic children in poor schools I were taught without payment of fees. Therefore Ihe was not going to speak against free education, and there was no danger of Catholics being on the I unpopular side in this matter. What he did speak lagainst was the holding out of free education as a bait to induce the working classes to send their children to secular schools. SIR RICHARD CROSS AND NEWTON DIVISION.--A paragraph having been circulated to the effect that Sir Richard Assheton Cross's chances of election for the Newton Division of South-West Lancashire were Very slight, and that the right honourable gentleman had earnestly asked to be put up for some other division of the county, a correspondent communicated with Sir Richard on the subject, and the following reply has been received Home Office, October 26, 188.5.—My Dear Sir,--I am much obliged by your letter. I can only say that the statement in the paper to which you allude— namely, that I earnestly asked to be put up for some other division of the county—is absolutely untrue. What I stated in my address, on the other hand, is as absolutely true, so is your conclusion that I had been asked by many other divisions. With the help Of friends like yourself, I mean to win.—:-Always sincerely yours, EICHA.RD ASSRETON CROSS.'

div.head: CFIURCIT DEFENCE MEETINGS AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: CFIURCIT DEFENCE MEETINGS AT WARRINGTON.

_ On Monday afternoon a conlerenoe of the clergy and laity of Warrington and the district was held in the Co- operative Hall, Sankey-street. The chair was ',coupled by the Rev. Canon Whitley, rector ef Newton-in•Makerfield. The proceedings were private, but we understand the follow. ing resolutions were carried :—Oo the motion of the Rev. Canon Greenall, sec-nded by the Rev. H. Monk, it was re- solved, "That a branch of the Church Defence Institution be formed for Warrington and the district, with a committee

consisting of six clergy and six laity." The names of the I clergy and laity forming the committee having been decided upon, on the motion of Mr. Seaton, seconded by the Rev. W. H. Williams, of Padgate, it was resolved, "That this confer- rence desires te call attention to the evasive character of the answers returned by many candidates for Parliament in this neighbourhood when challenged as to their opinions respect- ing the maintenance of the Established Church, and declines to accept the reason alleged for avoiding any definite ex- pression of opinion that the question did rot come within the range of practical politics." A vote 01 thanks to the chairman brought the meeting to a close. _

_ In the evening a meeting was held in the Assembly Room at the Conservative Club, Sankey-street, when an address was delivered by Mr. H. Byron Reed, a Parliamentary eau- didate for the division of Bradford. The chair was occu- pied by Mr. R. I. Wynne Jones, and amongst those present were the Revs. E. C. E. Carleton, S. Wilkinson, W. H. Wil- liams, T. P. Williamson, B. B. Prescott, J. G. Richards, F. Slater, T. S nith (Lowton), G. Anton, C. C Brown, I. Phillips, and J. Ward; Messrs. John White, Thomas Jolley, Henry Oreenall, James Fairclough, W. J Burgess, John Hatton, James Smethurst, D. W. Finney, P. W. Howson, H. J. Longton, John Dewharst, Thomas Hutchinson, Joseph Taylor, W. Richardson, _and J. Bolton. _

The CHAIRMAN said that meeting was not, AS they knew, a party political one, and he hoped there would be amongst them many Churchmen of all noir...cal opinions. (Applause.) He wished to say to them that they must re- member they were Churchmen first and policians afterwat ds —(applause)—that when the Church was attained politi- cally they were bound to defend her politically, and he wished to impress upon them most earnestly that at this time it was their bounden duty to ascertain the views of the candidates who would represent them in Parliament on the subject of disestablishruent and purely secular educa- tion in schools—which meant education that did not acknowledge even a God. They would have nothing to do with a man who, whether by his vote or by his abstention from voting, which was almost as had, countenanced in any measure what was meant to unchristaanise the Curchmen of England, and threaten the Established March. (Ap- plause.) Mr. H. BYRON REED, who was received with applause' said they had met that evening for serious and practical business. They were in the presence of a great attack upon an institution which they all held dear, dearer than anything this life could give them, and more precious to them than any programme that aspiring politicians could offer. (Hear, hear, and applause.) They were ia the presence of an attack upon their old National Church—an attack which

had been going on for a number of years,, but which ap- peared to be culminating in these times ; and the necessi- ties of the case demanded two or three steps being taken. First of all, they should make themselves acquainted with the nature of the attack; secondly, they should inquire into the results of the attack should it be successful ; and, thirdly, they should take counsel together as to the best means of dJeating the enemy all along tke line. (Applause.)—Mr. Josue WHITE proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Reed for his excellent, eloquent, and interest- ing address.—Mr. W. J. BURGESS seconded the proposal._ The Rev. E. C. E. Ch.RLETON, in supporting it, referring to Mr. William Crosfield, said that gentleman was a Liberationist, but be said as little as possible about the Church question in his addrese, and also as little as possible in his speeches. He remembered him making speeches in the different wards of the town some few months ago, and he watched carefully what he said, but he had not a word to say on the Church question, and that was the way these people did Many of them were trying to get into Parlia- ment by avoiding the question and misleading the people. The English people did not want a man in Parliament of whose opinions they knew nothing. That was not the way to gain the confidence of the electors. (Applause.) Mr. Carleton referred to the Parish Church which, he said had been built at a large cost for some of the poorest people in the town—the people of Sohool-brow, Mersey-street, and Howley Quay? It was their church, and they had the right to claim their seats at all times without being asked for pew rents. Was Mr. Crosfield to take the church from those poor people, and if he took it away what was he go- ing to give in its place? Was he going to build a magni- ficent Congregational chapel? Nothing of the kind. He did not propose even to spend a single sixpence in erecting a building for their use. The poor people to whom he had ' referred would want to know why they were to be robbed in that manner. Why should they lose their place of worship when the peeple of Wycliffe Chapel were to be un- disturbed? In what respect were the Congregationalists

„ as superior to everyone else that they should be treated in that exceptional manner ? (Applause.)—Tbe resolution was then put to the meeting and carried unanimously, and a vote of thanks having been accorded to the Chairman, and. "God save the Queen” sung, the proceedings terminated.
WARRINGTON INFIRMARY CONCERT.

The annual concert promoted by the Working Men's Infirmary Committee was held on Saturday evening in the Public Hall, there being, as usual, a crowded attend- ance. The chair was occupied by Major J. R. Pickmere. who, in the course of a few introductory remarks, said he had been asked by the Working Men's Committee to pre- side that evening, and it gave him a great deal of pleasure to d• an. He remembered presiding on the first occasion that the Committee gave their concert, and he well rec,llected the anxiety they had as to whether the concert would pay or not for the expenses of the hall, advertising, etc. On that occasion, however, they cleared a handsome sum for the Infirmary and Dispensary, end since then the amount had increased until now the Work- ing Men's concert was one of the institutions of the town. (Hear, hear, and applanee.) There were one or two facts in connection with the institution which he thought would be interesting to them. He might just say that the ides of the Warrington Infirmary was first entertained in 1874, a year in which he had the honour of being mayor of the borough in 1875 the foundation stone was laid, and in 1876 the infirmary and Dispensary was publicly opened by air Richard Cross. (Applause.) Since that time 29,000 cases had passed through the hands of the doctors of the Infirmary and Dispensary—he was speaking of the cases that had been attended to in the town, some at their own house and some at the Infirmary. That was a large number, rather more than 3,000 a year, no that they would see how much they were benefited by the inrtitution bleb they wore supporting by their p-esence that night. (Applause.) He thought the working men's corn- mittee and the working men in general deserved every credit for the manner in which they collected money by- concerts and other means in.support of the Infirmary— (hear, hear,)—and he would especially refer to the inde— fatigable secretary of the committee, Mr. Thomas Roberts. (Applause.) He thought also that gratitude was due to the committee, beth ladies and gentlemen, who had the manage- ment of the Infirmary, and to the doctor, who, be believed, was liked by all with whom he \ came into contact. Dr. Richmond had kindly favoured him with a few interesting statistics in reference to the institution from which he saw that in 1823 the income from all sources was 1.360, and of this the annual subscriptions reached the stem of £239. They would see, therefore, thee the entire income of tbe dispensary was then very lunch below the amount now con- tributed by the working men themselves; but of course the town bad now probably double the population it had then. In the balance sheet for 1823 there were some curious items, one of which was, "John Wright, for an assault, 55," and another item for an assault, presumably of a more serious nature, Ll. Amongst the payments were, "John Witt. moue, saving Whitlow's son, 55," and the next item was, "Peter Norris, saving Nash's child, 10a 61" Dr. Rich- mond had facetiously remarked that he supported the oiffer- mice in the amounts paid was due to "Nash's child" being a girl, and consequently.torth something more for saving. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) They would see that the institu- tion they were assembled in aid of that night had arisen from very small beginnings; and he was sure that the people of Warrington were proud of it and would do what they could to support it, however little their gifts might be. (Hear, hear.) There was one gentleman amongst them who after so many years toil in connection with the administratiOn must be gratified by the success which it had attained—he alluded to their friend Mr. Beamont. (Loud applause.)—The concert was then commenced by the band of the 9th (whose services had been granted by Colonel (ireenall) playing a selection of Scotch airs. This selection, as well as the other items contributed by the band, was played with admirable precision and was lc'udl7 applauded. Mr. McClure excellently rendered "The village black- smith," "Anchored," and "Pally"; and Miss Podmore was very successful in her two songs " Slagle " and s, The miller and the maid," for each of which she was warmly applauded. As might be expected, the hnmourous sketches of Mr. Harry Collins were the most appreciated. Mr. Col- lins manifested no little capacity as a humourist and his rendering of comic pieces won him:aeveral recoils. Miss Elise Hey, who made a favourable impression at last year's concert, sang three songs, "Tell ane,lny heart." "Oh. bow delightful," and "Home, sweet home," to each of which her voice of marked sweetness and power, and over which she has complete control, enabled her to do ample justice. Dr. Mapei, also one of last year's artistes, was cor- dially applauded for his rendering of 'O'er the hills of Normandie" and "Close to the Threshold" One of the best pieces of the evening was a duet, " I've wandered in dreams," by Miss Hey and Dr. Minot, which was a much admired performance. The band was under the conductor- ship of Mr. Thomas Armstrong, who, it is scarcely neces- sary to say, discharged his duties in a skilful and satisfac• tory manner. Much credit is due to Mr. G. Riley for the manner in which he accompanied the singers on the piano, and also for his gratuitous services in connection with the getting up Of this successful concert.

ip • MY AUTUMN QUEEN. 'Pd h. Come, weary little maiden, , With all thy laughter fled, ▪ . Two handl?, with berries laden, , Red berries on thy head, . With little step that lingers, 10• IL 7- ; Tired in the long, dusk road, aviict..t With droop of weary fingers„ ' Faint, w.th their ruddy load.;— , . Come, darling! let me carry • . This wealth thy heart desired;. r it Sure little footsteps tarry ' When little feet are tired. The eventide comes colder, And we must homeward hold, So lay thee on this shoulder , Thy head of ravelled gold. 0 maiden! thou.hadst led me, • As to a merry tune; • With twinkling feet that fled me All thro' the autumn noon. Yet when the air: was mellow And shade there Was noAe, When wdodS of red and yellow • Flashed in the fiery sun— v s sweet was thy fleeing laughter, In echo till more sweet, , t•" While noit leaves flattered" after The going of thy feet. , , • " Thou'ledst through rustled places, Where brown leaves.made their lair; Thou spedst down sunlit spaces, , With loose gold on thy hair. 4. Oh, we were'gay together, . This sunny maid and I, All in the autumn Weather, Beneath the autumn sky. % We wrought amid the sedges ••••• Green crowns of finest pith; • . We sought along the hedges • Red gems to twine therewith. WiNgreen and red I bound thee, Where sunlight set its sheen; I kissed, dear child, and crowned thee My shining Autumn Queen; ' A queen with sleep o'erladen, Whose crown droops from her head, This weary little maiden, With all her laughter fled. —JAMES• HENDRY, in Good Words.

Gay okl gentleman to boy, on twelfth birthday: "I I hope you Ni ill improve in wisdom, knowledge, and vir- tue Boy, politely returning compliment, totally un- I conseious'of sarcasm, "Thu same to you, sir." , From the universal law of habit, little by little, day .by day, act by act, thread by thread, link by link, we mould the character, we weave the woof, we forge the chains which bind our being and in forming our habits form our character. One of the results of the athletic sports is that the pedestrian fever has even extended to the most secluded precincts of the family circle. We hoar of several young ladies of highly respectable parents in the town who are training to walk, and nearly all of them are under two years of age. An eag,aged young gentleman got rather neatly out of a little serape with his intended. She said she had heard that he had kissed two ladies at some party at which she was not present. He owned it, but said, laughingly, that, after all, their united ages made only twenty-one. The simple-minded girl thought of ten and eleven, and laughed off her pout. He did not explain that one was aineteen and the other two years of age. John Davie, a, farmer in Walton, parish of Cardross, was remarkable for his ready turn of wit. One day, when returning home from Dumbarton with a, pig which he had purchased there, he met Major Alexander, then 'residing at Auchinf roe, who accosted him thus :--" Well, John, is this a cousin of yours you have got with yott to- day ?" to which John replied, "Deed, no sir; he's no' a trepnd ava, but only an acquaintance, like yourser." . A country clergyman was one day catechising his flock in the church. The bedral being somewhat ill-read in his "Carritch," thought it best to keep a modest place near the door, in the hope of eScaping the inquisition. But the,elergyman observing him, and divining his ob- ject, called him forward. "John," said he, "what is baptism ?" " Ou, sir," answered John, scratching his • head, "ye ken its just saxpence to me, and fifteenpenee to tale precentor." A New York man applied to Abraham Lincoln, some years before he became President, as to the financial standing of one of his neighbours. Mr. Lincoln replied as follows :—" Yours of the 10th inst. received. lam well acquainted with Mr. , ann know his circum- stance. First of all he has a wife and baby; together the-3, ought to be worth 50,000 dollars to any man. Se- condly, he has an office in which there is a table worth 1.50 dollars, and three chairs worth, say, one dollar. Last of all there is in one corner a large rat-hole which will bear. looking into.—Respectfully yours, A. Lnicotx." , .T}7g MEN WHO ARS PROMOTED.—The young men who receive promotion as the men who clo not drink on the They is not the men who are at the front when- ever there s a strike, nor are they the men who watch for the clock to strike 12, and leave their picks hanging in the air. They are the men usually who pay the closest attention to the details of their business, who act as if the,y were trying to work for their employer's interests instead of to beat him at every crook and turn. They are the men who give the closest attention to eVery de- tail, and who look continually to see whether they can do any better or not. This class of men are never out of a job. They are scarce. They never strike, they never loaf, and they do not ask for their pay two or three weeks before pay day. During a season of great drougiat the inhabitants of a certain parish in Essex—at leadd is said—sank a deep .well at the,publie expense. The well having been dug, the large heap of earth which had come out of it was by common consent voted an eyesore which ought to be removed. A parish meeting was accordingly held to consider haw the obnoxious heap should be got rid of. Mahy sngpestions were made as to the best way of deal- i'Vwith it, but at last it was proposed and unanimously carried that they should dig a large hole and bury it! Dow often the process of digging a fresh hole to bury the earth which had come out of the last hole was re- peated we never heard, but we fear the plan must have put the parish to a good deal of expense before it was suCeessfal, . PLEASANT I—An American acting manager tells the following -story, says the Era, in reference to the late General Grant: "The first act was over, and we were .chatting in the wings with our manager. when one of the boys rushed up to tell us that General Grant and fasuily were in one of the boxes. A flush of gratified pildg mounted to the managerial face, followed by a look. or agonised doubt as he evidently reflected that perhaps .the General had come in with an order. Did you send him a box, Robson?' be asked me, and on my replying in the r(egative,'he pulled a card out of his pocket. and, scribbling .a line on it, told the boy to take it to the box office, and bring back an answer. The boy rushed off, his, head full of the General, and returned in a few minutes with the. same card, which he handed to the manager. A ghastly look crossed his face as he read it, and without a word handed it to me. The first line read in the rather shaky managerial ealigraphy, 'Did Gen. Grant pay for his box? while underneath ap- peared, No. but may son Fred did. U. S. Grant.' the boy had taken it to the box instead of the box office." THE FOUR TRIALS.—There was once an old monk walking through the forest with a little scholar by his side. The old man suddenly stopped and pointed to four: plants close at hand. The first was beginning to peep above the ground; the second had rooted itself pretty well into the earth; the third was a small shrub; whilst the fourth arid last was a full sized tree. Then the old monk said to his young companion :—" Pull up the first." The youth easily pulled it up with his fingers. "Now pull the second. The youth obilyed, but not so easily. "and the third." Out the boy had to put forth all his strength, and use both arms, before he succeeded in up- rooting it. "And now,":said the master, "try your hand upon the fourth." , But lo! the trunk of the tall tree (grasped in the arms of the youth) scarcely shook its leaves; and the little fellow found it impossible to tear its roots from thmearth. Then the wise old monk ex- plained to his scholar the meaning of the four trials. This, my son, is just what happens with our passions. When they are young and weak, one may, by a little watchfulness over self, and the help of a little self-denial, easily tear them up; but if we let them cast their roots deep down into our souls, then no human power can up- root them, the almighty hand of the Creator alone can pluck them out. For this reason, my child, watch well ' over the first movements of your soul, and study by acts of virtue to keep your passions well hi check." ELECTRIC HOUSE BELLS.

It is the B..rface root we wish to protect, and in order to do so more effectually we advise that they should have two or three inches of mulching with de- cayed manure every year, an 4411 loose material annually moved before a fresh application is made. It is difficult to calculate when a pear or an apple tree will bear fruit when left to grow naturally and differently grafted, but

we remember an old proverb that says, Ile that planteth pears plantoth for his heirs." This may be a stretch of poetic imagination; but we are acquainted with both apple and pear trees, 10 years Old, that have never had fruit on. During the past season we noted the following apple trees, bearing beautiful fruit, in Mr. Moss's garden at Fulwood:--Worcester Pearmain, Rib- ston Pippin, Court-pen-du plat, Duchess Of Oldenburgh, Ecklinville Seedling, Irish Peach, Red Astrachan, Lord Derby, and Gloria Mundi, all superior sorts. Tim FRONT GrARDEIN.—BULBS.—AII kinds of spring floWering bulbs, such as Snowdrops, Crocuses, Nar- cissus, Tulips,- and Hyacinths are so extremely cheap that they all ought to be represented in the cottage garden. Those grown in pots in the window, it taken care off and .planted in May or June, will flower freely next 'spring. Now. is the time to secure imported bulbs, and from now to the middle of November is the best time to plant them, which Should be done in clumps and not frittered about, one here and another there. The diameter of the groupi may vary from 6in. to one foot when planted, which will be several inches more when grown up, and small bulbs should occupy the lesser space. The soil, if not unusually good, should be thrown out to the depth of the spade, and thatbelow stirred up, and some thoroughly,. decayed manure mixed with it. Chopped turfy lOam and decayed manure would be an excellent compost to Mahe holes; and would well repay the la.benr,expended...' , TrniWmnow.-Thereare various spring-flowering bulbs .which, if potted about this time, will make a grand show in the vvindow at that seaSon,"and the Jonquils, Nar- cissus, and Hyacinths -are highly scented. But the gayest of all is the Tulip. • The Hyacinth are Potted singly, in Pots 4in. to 'Gin, diameter, but the others are placed three to five in that size pot, and the Narcissus are,usually provided..with 7in. or 81n. pots. The soil that will suit one will do for the others, and the best no doubt is a cost of rich loam and leaf mould, to which ' may be added' One-eighth decayed manure, , free from worms and dt er insects also as much sand ai will give tile Whole 'a sandy appearance. The Chairman, who was warmly, received, said he was occupying the chair in 'consequence of 'the absence of Mr.' Joseph Evans, their president. 'He had very great pleasure in taking the chair on such an occasion as that, and he {di very much honoured in presiding on the occasion of Colona MeCorquedale's first appearariels at a public meeting since, his acceptance of the candidature of the division. (AD.' plauae.) He need not go into ' the, history of the franchise question, and the measure which had brought them there, ot tell them how the Liberals beat the Tories in the House of Commons and House of Lords, and thereby gave them a vote. (Applause.) He explained the work and for- mation of the Executive Committee, and proceeded to nay that when the executive had looked about them for a suitable man they found their decision narrowed to a small limit and their choice made remarkably easy, because one man stood out beyond all others as the best candidate, they could possibly find. (Cheers.) He need not tell them who that gentleman - 'ee hun- dred was then called repre- sentatives from all , ' Col. McCorquodale to alt that meeting was tbal mouely as their calitU up against tne NOte plause.) He (the el all the candidates standing t er man more honourably and chosen by any coostituencY vas for the Newton Divisi INV his politics and his privi; . been amongst them, and they knew be was not.a man who wonld run away from them. Applause.) That was the reason why the executive and the "300" had chosen him, aid be- 'cause he wee a local man acquainted .with the requirements of the district, and theyjelt that they &mid trust him. (Applause.) . Colonel McCorquodale, J.P., on rising t) address the meeting, was' greeted with cheers, repeatedly renewed. lie. said headesired to thank the chairman for the kind expres- eions be had made use of in informing them how the choice of candidate came about six months ago, and he felt grateful to them for the enthuelasin they had ishowo,and trusted that the campaign in which t they were engaged would be carried., on in an orderly and fair manner. (Applause.) AftAr ex- plaining that the delay carved in addressing bia constitaents was owing to the inconsistency of his opponent.; with whores an understanding had been arranged as to the opening of the contest, Colonel McCorquodale said his attention had recently been drawn to a speech delivered by Mr. Pardey, the agent of Mr. William John Legh, who had Int de a charge that he (Colonel McCorquodale) had attended a cer- tain meeting and endorsed certain viewe, and had made it so clear that there seemed to, be no, getting out ef it— (laughter)--except in this, way, that there was not the slightest foundation for. one word that was contained in that speech further than that he was at the meeting id question. The chairman of that Conservative meeting had alluded to Sir Richard Cross's election:address. of which he (Colonel .McCorquodale) also had a copy, hot be could not understand his opponent's views on the question Of educa- tion, and me would defy any person in that room to under- stand what Sir R. Cross meant. (Hear, boar, and laughter.) In his opinion Sir R. Cross would do whatever be liked if he went into Parliament, because he was not bound in the slightest way: Referring to certain remarks of Mr. West- bead, the chairman of the Newton Polling District Consee- vative Club, Col. McCorquodale said that gentleman had re- ferred to religion, to what he tented atheists at noon end as- sassins at dead of night, and so forth. (Laughter.) Well, he (Colonel McCorquodale) did not think there were any in Eariestown, or Newton, or in Golborne: (Hear, hear.) Then he finished up by saying they should have as their motto, " Fear God and honour the Qneen." Now, it was very well for Mr. Westhead to say that, but perhaps he took it from his (the speaker's) 'house, where for over quarter of a century he had had, over his fireplace those words, in the original form, " Fear God, honour the King," of which he had taken ,a tracing. (The production of the tracing was received with loud cheers.) He did not know any other house in the Newton Division where these words were put up for their daily guidance. Perhaps there were some; at any rate he hoped so. He bad also placed near to these words the golden rule of doing unto others as he would wish them to do unto us. Thrmigh. I out that contest he hoped there would be no personalities. I He suggested this at Wigan, and the idea was faithfully I carried out. (Hear, hear.) He had made these preliminary observations of a personal character, for he MO bound to clear the way. With regard to Gelborne he might mention that some months ago the chairman of the Conservative . Association was reported to have said that Colonel ; WCorquodale Yeas a personal friend of his (the chairman); but he did not think he was seeking to enter Parliament so much in the belief that he could bring about any great benefit to the country as he was anxious to advance the •, personal position of the members of his family.. This, of I course, was not said out ef any disrespect. '(Cries of " Shame "). Now, speaking at Earlestown in April last, he (Colonel MlCorquodale) said:—" He put his business, family, and personal matters, all on one tide, and his duty to the Liberals of that division and to the 'Liberal party generally on the other side, and Came to the determination I to sacrifice personal convenience for dates He was new , before them to carry out that determination, and to do his I best to serve them at the election." (Cheers.) It was for ! the electors to consider whether he had been quite properly', treated or not. He was not going to express any opinion. • VOTERS AND THEIR VOTES. Sir,—Both Conservative and Liberal orators are always impressing upon us how very responsible a trust the right of giving a Parliamentary vote is. They very truly tell us that the House of Commons is the great National Council, and that any inability on its part to deal with the very im- portant business that comes before it might have results which would prejudicially affect every individual in the country. Now as the House of Commons is composed of Individuals, and its business capacity is neither more nor less than the combined capacity of its members, the very Proper moral these orators draw is that each constituency, if it desire that the country should be wisely governed, should select the most capable man it has the choice of. To those voters who are not pledged to either party I would, therefore, give the advice to attend one or two meetings of both parties, and judge of the qualities of the respective can- didates for themselves. I venture topredict that after they have listened to one of Mr. Crosfleld's speeches they will come to the conclusion that if he has one strong point it is his ability to treat a subject in a shrewd and business-like way. I will not attempt to characterise Sir Gilbert's method of dealing with public questions. I will only ask these electors who wish to make an honest and patriotic use of their votes, that, after they have heard the Conservative candidate speak, they may put to themselves the questions: Would they be willing to entrust their private affairs to a man who showed as little comprehension of those affairs as Sir Gilbert Greenall does of the great public questions of the day? Would they like the municipal interests of the town to he managed by men who babbled in the same way as Sir Gilbert Greened'? And, finally, I ask them to picture to themselves a House of Commons composed of Sir Gil- bert Greenalls. Afrer they have done that lam sure they will come to the conclusion that though Conservative wire- pull-rs may show an abject deference to money-bazs and beer-barrels. there is no necessity for independent electors , to insult their intelligence by voting for their nominee.— Yours, Lc., AN INDEPENDENT.

TORY SL kNDERING.

Sir,—Toryism in Warrington must be in a wretched con- dition when it has to resort to the wholesale slandering of Its opponents. The slimy little publication which does duty as the organ of the Warrington Tories, has been cast- ing about for a set of to the intimidation reported as being practised at the Crewe works, and has insinuated that I do the same thing at Whitecross, and that I worked the men overtime to prevent their attending the Tory meeting, while the fact is that several Tories who expressed a wish were allowed to go half an hour before six o'clock, the usual stopping time. It is time the respectable members of the Conservative party entered their protest against this vile system of mud throwing with the hope that some of it may stick. If they do not, the public will hive just cause to look upon them as participators in the dirty work.— Yours, &c, THOMAS BIRC HALL.

div.head: WARRINGTON ELECTION.
div.p: WARRINGTON ELECTION.

Sir.—'The sounds of polit)cal warfare are thickening all around us, and it now behoves the elect-s of our good old town "to consider the relative merits of the two can. didates who are asking their suff rages. On the one hand we have our " old and tried friend " Sir Gilbert Greenall, and on the other Mr. William Crosfield, a comparatively new and ur.tried man. The one hata past to refer to—the other has only promises of future service to offer us. In this, if no other, the latter is the most promising man. Sir G. Greenall, has, I say, a past to refer to—although he I very seldom does so except in very general terms, as the record offers nothing very brilliant to boast of. His political virtues were of the negative kind, and so were his short- comings, for he left undone many things we think he ought to have done. When in Parliament he was a political ne- gation—a Parliamentary nothing—merely the stop-gap member for Warrington, who never, except as the tool in a piece of Benjamin's political trickery, never, I say, 80 much as lifted his finger to enfranchise the voters whom he now so earnestly beseeches to favour him. But in this he is entirely at one with the rest of the Tory candidates, who with faces of brass and consciences of lead, are pleading at the feet of the newly enfranchised—the very men they 80 lately held at arm's length and treated with contemptuous contumely —as the herd, the dross, the residuum. It_ must indeed require a face of brass to aik for that from a man which you had previously done your best to prevent him obtaining. The candidature of this brewer knight is a discredit to all concerned—to himself, to his supporters, and to the borough, It is a discredit to himself, for if he has any eelf•knowledge he must know his own utter incapacity to fitly represent this important bor- ough. If he wishes to be convinced of this let him, with an impartial mind, read his own inane platform platitudes, the feeble twaddle that passes for a Speech, where instead of the burning topics of the day we are treated, ad nauseam, to reiterated statements as to "the pleasure! have in seeing around me" Captain this and Major that, do. The can- didature is a discredit to those who instigate and those who support it, knowing, as they must know, how Very much out of pace he is as a politician. He has one qualifica- tion and only one—money, and knowing this they still wish to foist upon us the senile inanities of an octogenarian, whom in his best days his own party regarded merely as a stop gap. But these ill-counsellers could not have prevailed had they not in his own breast a most powerful backer in the eager longing the old man has to relieve his local insig- nificance by being made a somebody at St. Stephees. Then, again,! say this candidature is a discredit and an. insult to the electors. It is equivalent to saying that anything is good enough for them, eves this political nullity, the elec- tion of whom would leave the town practically unrepre- sented, and serve only to counteract the vote of a better man.—l am, sir, faithfully yours, JOHN PEERS. Penketh, October 27, 1885.
THE CANDIDATES FOR ST. HELENS AND THE TEMPERANCE QUESTION.

Sir,—On behalf of the Great heart Lodge 1.0.G.T., and C.A. for Stopping the Sale of Intoxicating Liquors on Sun- day, I shall be obliged if you will insert in your paper the following letter addressed to the candidates for the St. Helens division, and their reply.—Yours truly, JAMES BIRD, Electoral Superintendent. St. Helens, Octoh.r 29tte, 1885. 80, Phythisn-street, St. Helens, 0,1. 20th, 185. _

Sir,—lt is my duty as Electoral Superintendent on be- half of the Great Heart Lodge 1.0.G.T., and also of the Central Association for Stopping the Sale of Intoxicating Liquors on Sunday, to bring the matter of temperance legislation before the two candidates for the representatioa of the St. Helens division in Parliament. I append three questions, and shall be glad to receive your early reply to them ; but at the same time I beg to ask your permission to publish the correspondence in the local papers.—l am, yours truly, _ _ _
JAMES BIRD, E. Supt.

Ist, Are you' in favour of closing public bou'ses entirely on Sundays? 2nd, Are you, in favour of giving to the ratepayers of any district the direct veto as regards the issue of new and renewal of existing licenses for the common sale ef intoxicating liquors? 3rd, Do you recognise vested interests in licensed premises after the expiration of the period for which such premises are licensed for the sale of intoxicants, and if so, do you propose giving compensa- tion?

div.head: RPLT.
div.p: RPLT.

Roby Hall. Liverpool, Oct. 22, 1835. Dear sir,—l duly received your letter on the subject of temoerawe legislation, with the three questions enclosed. I am quite aware of the importance of the temperance ques- tion, and am willing to support any measure that will re- duce temptation to drink without unduly interfering with the liberty of the subject, and I desire to give the matter may most earnest consideration. But the practical difficul- ties in the way of "Sunday closing "and "local option" at present prevent my pledging myself unreservedly to support them. Can public-horses be entirely closed on I Sundays without tyranny? And can a system of local option be established that will be entirely free from jobbery and corruption ? When these questions are definitely an- swered, I shall be in a position to give a definite pledge. I an in favour of the principle that fair pecuniary com- pensation should be given to licensed victuallers and the owners of licensed property for depreciation in the value of such property resulting from future legislation. Whilst fully recognising the national evil of intemperance. I be- lieve that its cure lies as much in the sphere of social and religieus influence as in the field of politics.—l am, yours faithfully, _
H. SETON-KARR.
To Mr. James Bird, St. Helens. P.B.—You are quite at liberty, so far as I am concerned, publish this correspondence. H. S. K.
Colonel Gamble, J.P , has given his promise to a deputation which waited upon him to support. the bills, but I have received no,answer yet.—Youre, J. BIRD.

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, OCTOBER-31, 1885
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, OCTOBER-31, 1885
• KNITTSFORD DIVISION. MR. BARLOW AT PRESTON BROOK. Mr. J. Emmott Barlow, the Liberal candidate for the Snutsford Division, is carrying on a vigorous campaign. In
addition to bolding numerous meetings in town and coun-

try, at which he delivers effective and practical speeches, Mr. Barlow is conducting a personal canvas, and although he is opposed by one of the scions of the great Cheshire house of Egerton, his chances of success are very bright. A short time ago Mr. Barlow said Knutsford was one Of the two divisions which were supposed to be gifts to the

Tories,but he firmly believed that they would do better than in some of the divisions that were pointed out as strongholds of Liberalism. On Monday night a Conservative meeting was held at Daresbury, under the presidency of Sir Gilbert Greenell, and the Radical sentiment prevailed to such an extent, that the sturdy cheers given for Mr. Gladstone, Mr. Chamberlain. and other prominent Liberal leaders, and the groans for the opposite party, upset the equilibrium of the Walton baronet. He designated the Liberals present as wild beasts, and other choice epithets were applied to them, which had not a very good effect upon the proceedings. Although several present desired to ask questions of the candidate, the lion. Alan de Tatton Egerton, they were not permitted to do so, and the proceedings were altogether of a very " lively " character. It is an open question whether the resolution of support was carried, or not. The Liberals desired to hold a meeting in the same place on Tuesday evening, and Sir Gilbert Greenall promised them the use of the room. When, however, arrangements were to be made the tenant of the hotel to which the building is attached refused to allow a Radical demonstration to take place there. Tbie display of intolerance, however, was futile to prevent the demonstra- tion. Mr. T. Priestman, of the tannery, Preston Brook, placed a abed at the works at the disposal of the party, and this was transformed into an admirable meeting room. On Tuesday night it was filled with an enthusiastic assembly, notwithstanding the very boisterous state of the weather. Mr. G. Rodger, of Newton Bank, presided, and amongst those nresent were—Messrs. J. E. Barlow, the candidate, T. Priestman, Thomas C. Ellis (Northwich), T. Handley, B. IRniveton, J. Handley (Runcorn), J. Frodsham, W. Whit- low. J. Johnson, Grounds, John Jones, Lukes, Thomas Webb, R. Marshall, T. P. Taylor. &c. In a brief speech the Camensuat introduced Mr. BARLOW, who delivered a speech which was listened to with earnest attention. He apologised for having so long neglected to come to Preston Brook, but he was in- formed that the people there were so well informed in every- thing that appertained to Liberalism that it would be a waste of time to come near them at all. (Hear, hear.) By , quotations from speeches by prominent Tory statesmen, he showed how the extension of the franchise was opposed ' tooth and nail by the Conservative party. (Cheers.) They were sometimes told that the last five years of Liberal Government had been particularly adverse to all the in- terests of the country and that trade had been very bad. He admitted at once that trade and commerce had not been as good as it might have been, and he was sorry for that fact, because it interested himself. The trade of the country Was, however, very much better while the Liberals were in office than during the previous five years of Tory rule. Taking the whole trade of the country there were during the five Liberal years nearly 400 millions mere of exports and imports thaa there were in the Con- servative time. (Cheers.) He was afraid that the trade was not carried on at a very large percentage of profit but it was carried on, and it provided employment for the people of the nation. (Cheers.) Never in the history of the cotton trade had there been so large an amount of wages paid to the operatives in Lancashire as there Was during the last five years. (Cheers.) There were seven million tons of iron and steel exported more than in the previous five years. (Hear, hear.) There was one thing in which the Tories beat the Liberals, and that was in the number of bankruptcies. (Loud laughter, and cheers.) They had 9,000 more bankruptcies in those five years of office than had the Liberals in theirs. (Laughter.) He pointed out the large decrease of pauperism during the Liberal administration, and showed that during the last 20 years the Liberals, who had been eleven years in office, diminished taxation by 28,1 millions, RII4 the Tories, during their nine years of office, increased taxation by 31 millions. (Cheers.) He declared himself in favour of County Boards elected by the ratepayers by ballot, each ratepayer to have one vote. (Cheers.) He was in favour of Free Educatior. (Cheers.) He would have an inquiry into the institutions in London and throughout the country, founded for the benefit of the poor people and now carried on to minister to the luxuries of the privileged few : and he would apply the funds towards giving the people free education. (Cheers.) If the fonds were more than were required he would provide technical schools so that the men of this country could acquire a technical knowledge of the handicrafts in which they were engaged, and thus com- pete more successfully. with the people of other countries. (Hear, hear.) It was by measures of this kind, and not by a return to the obsolete fallacies of Protection, that we we should have an England which would be greater and more powerful, happy and more prosperous, than the England of to-day. (Cheers.) Mr. P. SCRAGO asked a question, which he said he was not allowed to ask at the Tory meeting at Daresbury. (A voice : "Shame for them." Another voice : "Three cheers for Greenall." Loud groans. "And for his ale." Renewed groans.) In answer to questions, Mr. BARLOW said he was in favour ef the ratepayers of a locality having the power to say whether or not they would have public houses. (Cheers.) Mr. PRIESTMAN, who was loudly cheered, moved "That this meeting having heard Mr. J. E. Barlow, considers him to be a fit and proper person to represent the Knutsford Division in Parliament, and pledges itself to use all legiti- mate means to secure ble return." A WORKINGMAN in the audience seconded the resolution. Mr. B. KNIVETON supported the resolution in a speech which frequently elicited cheers. He argued that nine out of every ten great measures calculated to raise and elevate the people of England were Liberal measures carried by the Liberal party, and opposed by the Tories. (Cheers.) Mr. T. C. ELLIS also supported the resolution in a hu- mourous speech. Mr. W. HANDLEY delivered an address bristling with facts and figures put in an intelligible and interesting form. He pointed out that if the cost of Free Education was borne out of the local rates the charge upon the working man would be four times less than the present system of school fees, which in many cases entailed so much hardship. He. how- ever, did not think it would be paid for by this means. He believed that a great portion of the cost csuld be supplied by an improved system of collection of taxation. (Hear, hear.) The education, he believed, would have to be paid for by Imperial taxation and the consolidated fund. (Hear, hear.) In a certain part, not two hundred miles away—(a laugh)— where there was £1,200 collected in custom duties, the salaries amounted to £BOO. (" Shame.") Was not there room for saving there, and would not it look better to pay a good portion of that towards the education of children? (Cheers.) He was confident that if Free Education was taken up sea Parliamentary question, the ways and means would be found, and that it would not be any burden what- ever, or a scarcely-felt burden, on the country at large. (Cheers.) As a Guardian of the poor he could confidently state that the whole tendency of the system of application of school fees was downward. —(hear, hear)—and the Liberal party having for the last fifty years endeavoured to educate the people were not going to advocate or retain a policy ef that kind. (Cheers.) There were plenty of our rich people who got their chil- dren educited free. It was not long since be heard of a gentleman offering another gentleman £lOO if he would get his son into Christ's Hospital, London, the education there was so good and free. The man got the £lOO, and the son of a wealthy man was educated free. Let them, he said, take the revenues of these institutions which were founded for the benefit of the poor and put them to their original use, and not for the exclusive use of the rich. Cheers) The motion was carried with loud cheering, there not be- ing a dissentient hand held up. Mr. Banaow briefly replied, and the meeting con- cluded.
ferred to the much vaunted treaty of Berlin, now, he said,

crumbled to pieces, Mr. Barlow referred to a statement or Mr. Egerton that Lord Salisbury's Government came into office fettered with the chains forged by the late Govern- ment, but that the Afghan boundary question had been set- tled. It had been settled precisely upon the lines laid down

by Mr. Gladstune's Govern' Inent-L(aPolause)—without one jot or one tittle of variation. They were told that Mr. Egerton would support the present Government in restoring the Navy to such a position as would secure our vast com- mercial interests. He (Mr. Barlow) was quite prepared to say that he supported not only the present, but any Gov- ernment, in putting the Navy into a proper position. Mr. Egerton said "I am in favour of granting to Ireland such measures of local government as can be safely entrusted to her." It seemed that Mr. Egerton thought one measures of local government could not be safely entrusted to Ire- land. For his (Mr. Barlow's) part, he was in favour of giv- .

ing to Ireland focal government as mush as to England. (Hear, hear.) He saw no reason to suppose that Irishmen were particularly :Weep when their own interests were con- cerned, and he could see no reason why Irishmen should be brought to settle their affairs in London, and that the people in Cheshire should be able to have county boards and settle their's in Cheshire. Mr. Eger- ton said he would be glad to support any measure having for its object the decentralisation of local government, and which, by developing local talent and energy would enable many questions to be entrusted to a duly constituted local authority. They should inquire what that authority was likely to be. When the Conser- vatives were in °free they brought forward two bills to give local government in the counties. One was brought in in 1878 by Mr. Sclater Booth, who said that the Government ' had determined wpon a plan identifying the County Board with the Court of Quarter Sessions. In other words, ' they meant to call the magistrates a County Board, and that was their idea of a reform. That was a failure., and , afterwards they proposed that a third of the members of a county beard should be ex-officio justices, and two-thirds elected representatives, but that was too Radical a measure for their friends and supporters, and they then said they would have eae-half ex officio magistrates and the other half should be elected by the Guardians. (Laughter.) But for fear this body should eet into mischief they would take from it every item of county government: they would leave the Board stranded with nothing to do. His (Mr. Barlow's) opinion was that such a Board should be elected upon the principle that every ratepayer should have a vote, and should exercise it by ballot. (Ap- plause.) Mr. Egerton was not prepared to consent to the disestablishment and disendowment of the English Church, and Mr. Barlow did not know who else was at the present moment. Mr. Gladstone bad told them that he did not ex- pect to see it during his life. Mr. Chamberlain said that we should not have it this Parliament, and therefore it would not be brought forward as a Government measure. Refer- ring to another item in Mr Egerton's address, Me Barlow said that he firmly believed that universal free education would not destroy voluntary schools, nor would it do away with religious training in such schools. Mr. Egerton also said that he wee anxious to see the transfer of land made as easy as the transfer of any other property, but be could not consent to a policy of confiscation which would compel landowners to sell against their will. Why, at pre- sent, owners of land were compelled to sell against their will, for railways and other purposes. IA Voice : Ship Canal.) If it was not confiscation in that instance, why should it be confiscation to compel owners of land to sell at a fair price for the good of the community ? (Ap- plause.) Mr. Egerton also said that he would give hearty support to all measures that would really assist the agricul- tural labourer to earn higher wages and improve his posi- tion in life. (Applause.) Mr. Egerton, speaking at Higher Fearer, said that as a rule they would find that if wealth I was placed in one or two hands it was well and wisely utile, iced for the benefit of their fellow subjects. (Laughter.) The wag, it appeared, to improve the position of the work- ing-man was to place wealth in one or two hands, and then he would be 'at the charity or the caprice of the one or two ! Mr. Egerton said he could not forget that there were interests to be considered as well as those of the agricultural labourers. It seemed to him that in the pest Mr. Egerton and the Conservative party had Very well remembered the interests that were not those of the agrieultural labourers. There was one matter which the Conservatives were a little anxious to bring in again, and that was something in order le prefeet the price of wheat Some years ago, when the corn laws were in existence, the times were very bard for labouring men. The worst was felt in the South of England, where the people were so frightened at the idea of anything like a return to those hard times that they were determined, come what would, to vote against any man who would go in for a protective duty upon corn. In answer to questions, Mr. Barlow said they had it upon the authority of the members of the Government that Disestabliehment would not be introduced before another general election, and he could not imagine that any Government, hav- ing so pledged itself, could introduce one. With regard to tithes, he said that in Borne parts of the south of England, owing to tithes, land had had to go out of cultivation because it could not pay the tithe, let alone the rent, and that in some parts of the South the tithe had amounted to more than the rent. When tithe was the cause of land going out of cultivation, some means must be found to relieve it of the burden, as it was of national im- portance that the land should be put under cultivation. " Would you vote for the abolition of the House of Lords ?" He did not think anyone proposed to abolish the House of Lords unless that House set itself in opposition to the whole nation—(A. Voice: They have done)—and he cer- tainly was not going to be a party to setting up a echeme to bring about its abolition, as that would involve another general election on she subject. His impression regarding compulsory vaccination, was simply that cumulative penal- ties should be abolished. Mr. JAMES WHITLEY proposed "That this meeting con- siders Mr. John Einmot Barlow to Nee fit and proper person to represent the Knutsford Division of Cheshire in Perna- meet, and pledges itself by every lawful means to secure his return." (Applause.) He bad pleasure in doing so be- cause Mr. Barlow belonged to the party of freedom and progress, which bad given to working-men the ballot and the franchise, that had repealed the corn laws, and given a free press, and that had promised to give free education to the working-man's children, and to which they looked for the greeting of local option aad the closing of public- houses on Sundays. (Applause.) The resolution was seconded and carried, and a vote of thanks to the chairman, proposed by Mr. &mow, and seconded by Mr. W. Learn, was then passed. Subsequently a committee of Liberals of the district, with Mr. White- head as secretary, was formed, and the meetirg then con- cluded.

div.head: FORTHCOMING LIRERAI MEETINGS.
div.p: FORTHCOMING LIRERAI MEETINGS.

It will be seen from our advertisement columns that a mass meeting of Liberals will be held in the Public Hall, Warrington, next Wednesday evening, in sup- port of the candidature of Mr. W. Crosfield for the borough, and of C.louel McCorquodale for Newton Division. Mr. J. G. McMinnies, is to preside. In addition to the two candidates, the speakers will include Mr. S. Smith, M.P., and Mr. Joseph Howes. Meetings of Mr. Crosfield's supporters will on Thurs- day evening be held in Brick-street School-room, and on Friday evening in the Old Wesleyan School-room, Buttermarket-street. On Wednesday speakers of note will address a large meeting at Knutsford ; Mr. I. S. Leadam,"; Liberal candidate for Altrincham Di- vision, will speak to-day (Saturday) at Baguley, and on Tuesday at Brinksway, and on Wednesday he and Mr. T. G. Ashton, Liberal candidate for the Hyde Division. will speak at a meeting at Hazel Grove. Col. McCorquodale will address various meetings in' the Newton Division, and on Tuesday evening a meet— ing in support of Mr. Maspra,tt, Liberal candidate for ' the Widnes Division, will be held in the Drill Hall of that place; some exeellent speakers are expected to be present.

div.head: EXPLOSION AT NEWTON.
div.p: THE EXPLOSION AT NEWTON.

The terrible explosion of a revolving straw-boiler at the works of Messrs. Gillespie and Mason, paper manufacturers, Newton, ort Thursday week, formed the chief topic of conversation throughout the district last week end. Its disastrous consequences in the destruction of property were much commented upon. The work of removing the debris and mass of bricks, slates, and machinery was commenced early on Friday morning. The dead body of William Byrne, a married man, residing in Alfred-street, Newton, was discovered on the night of the explosion, but that of William Fleming, a single man, residing in Back Market-street, Earl.stown, was not found until half Past eleven on Friday forenoon. He was found lying in the demolished .4 poacher-room," where he was last seen alive. The whole of the injured men have since made rapid progress towards recovery. The remains of the two men, Wm. Bryne and Wm. Fleming, were interred in the grave-yard attached to the Roman Catholic Chapel, Crow-lane, on Monday afternoon.
