div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.

THE ALLEGED MURDER OF AN IRISH LABOURER. —At the Borough Court on Monday, John Scanlen, the Irish labourer who was last week brought be- fore the borough magistrates charged, on suspicion, with, in company with others, murdering another Irish labourer named Michael Ward, and remanded, was allowed to go on entering into his own recog- nisances of £4O to appear if called upon. It was stated that no trace of the missing man had been found, and that the result of the inquiries made was favourable to the prisoner. THE PAYMENT OF CORONERS' JuntEsl—On Sat- urday, on the conclusion of an inquest held at the White Hart Hotel, in Sankey-street, the foreman of the jury remarked that he thought men who were summoned to sit on a jury—who were generally men of business and who had to leave their work— should receive some remuneration for their services. Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy-coroner, who con- ducted the inquiry, concurred in these remarks. He had, he said, always advocated the payment of jury- men, and thought every man should be paid for his , services. The subject, which has many times been I ventilated at previous inquests, was then allowed to

drop. THE FATALITY ON THE RAILWAY.—The death of John Clifton (24), a porter, employed at the goods station of the London and North-Western Railway, Bank Quay, which occurred under circumstances already reported, formed the subject on Saturday of a coroner's inquiry, which was held at the White Hart Hotel, Sankey-street, before Mr. W. T. Hus- band and a jury. On the Thursday evening previ- ous deceased and a man named Clarke were engaged in shunting, when deceased was knocked down and run over by an engine. He was removed to the hospital, where he died shortly after his admiskon. A verdict of "Accidental death was returned. It is stated that the friends of the deceased obtain £BO from the Accident Fund.

RUNAWAY Boys.—Two boys named Frederick Smith (17) and Joseph Rose (15), the former the son of a bookseller and watchmaker living at Chorl- ton-on-Medlock, and the latter the son of a coach- man residing at Manchester, were charged on Monday at the Borough Court with being in posses- sion of two silver watches that were supposed to have been stolen. The father of Smith informed the Bench that his son had run away from home, taking the watches with him. He had induced the younger prisoner to accompany him, and the two came to Warrington, where they tried to sell one of the watches, as they were then without money. The father desired not to prosecute, and the boys were dismissed and handed over to their friends.

FINE FEATHERS " DON'T " MAKE FINE MIMS. —At the Borough Court, on Monday, a showily- dressed woman named Jane Daley, was summoned for using obscene language to another woman named Margaret Moriarty, in Old-road, Latchford, on the 15th inst. Mr. A. Browne, who appeared for complainant, explained that the principle cause of trouble between the parties appeared to be the in- congruity of the dress of one of the complainant's daughters, who wore a fur tippet and clogs. The language alleged to have been used by defendant having been given in evidence, the Mayor (Alder- man Harrison), who presided, said that it seemed almost impossible that a woman who wore such a fine feather in her hat as did defendant, should make such remarks. That was certainly incongru- ous. Defendant was ordered to be bound over to I keep the peace. ALLEGED EXTRAORDINARY OUTRAGE.—EarIy on Monday morning, P.C. Taylor, of the Borough police, was on duty in the vicinity of the Horse and Jockey Inn, Winwick-road, when he met a man who gave the name of Martin Hynes, coming from the direction of Winwick. The man had no hat, and his clothes were wet. The constable asked him what was the matter, and Hynes replied that he had been thrown over Longford Bridge into the brook, by three men. He was then taken to the police station, where he stated that he was a farm labourer, in the employ of Mr. William Falkner, farmer, Kenyon. lle came; he said, to Warrington on Sunday to visit some friends. He was walking back home when he saw three men standing on Longford Bridge. One of them asked him for a match, and he made reply that be had not one. Thereupon one of them said "Let's chuck him over the bridge." They then got hold of him, and carried the suggestion out. Hynes got out of the water, and made his way back to Warrington. When met by the constable he was sober. He was very much exhausted, and his wants were attended to by the police, _

SHOCKING ACCIDENT.—A foreman joiner, named Richard Campbell (44), who was in the employ of Messrs. Collin and Son, builders and contractors, Academy-street, and who lived in Dutton-street, I met his death in a shocking manner on Wednes- day. lie was engaged at a new building in course of erection in Bridge-street. He was seen standing at a window on the third storey pulling down the chain of the crane, when he was observed to suddenly throw outhis hands as if to catch the chain, and fall out of the window to the ground, a distante of about 30 feet. He was dreadfully injured, and died almost immediately. Deceased was a married man, and leaves a wife and family, for whom much com- miseration is felt. On Friday afternoon an inquest was held by Mr. Husband, deputy coroner, at the Seven Stars, Bridge-street, when evidence was given to the above effect. William Marnon, a labourer, said he had been in charge of the crane until within a few minutes of deceased's death, when by his permission he went down the building. On going back again somebody shouted that Campbell had fallen down. The crane was in proper working i order immediately before the accident and after it.l as well. Deceased was well liked by his fellow- workmen, and was perfectly sober at the time of the accident. A verdict of " Accidental death " was returned.

Doors open to Ticket.holcers at 8-45, and to the Public at 7-20, • TO THE ELECTORS OF THE WIDNES DIVISION OF SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE. GSISTLEMEN,—.The General Council of the Liberal Asso- ciation has unanimously elected me as the Liberal Candi- date for the Widnes Division of South-West Lancashire. I feel, therefore, that it becomes my duty, notwithstanding weighty private considerations which would lead me to de- stine, to accept the invitation to contest the seat in the Liberal interest at the coming Election. My political opinions are. I believe, generally known to you, as I have taken an active part in public affairs in Liverpool and Widnes, and from the unanimity of the vote in the District Councils, I gather that they are gen- erally acceptable to the Liberal party in the Division. I hope to have the pleasure of addressing meetings in each district, when I shall explain fully my views on these subjects which are likely to come prominently before the next Parliament. I need hardly say that, although I desire to advance fur- ther in some directions. I cordially support the policy in- dicated in Mr. Gladstone's address to the Electors of Midlothian, and that I appeal confidently to the Electors of our Division, who owe their enfranchisemeat mainly to the exertions of the Liberal Party and its great leader. for their support on the polling day. THE LAND Levis. As regards the laws relatiog to land, among other re- forms. I am in favour of prohibiting the settlement ot land upon unborn persons. and of the general power of creating life estates in land, the imendment of the law of landlord and tenant in a manner to promote and further protect Improvements, and such measures as may after discussion be found expedient to facilitate the acquirement of land for residence and cultivation. EDUCATION. If we are to meet successfully the competition of other nations in talanutacturing industry, our system of Educa- tion. both primary and secondary, must be improved. As one of the main causes of irregularity of attendance in primary schools Is the payment of school fees. I hope to see them abolished; and jam of opinion this can be done without injury, and indeed with benefit in poor districts. to voluntary or denominational schools, by means of an Increased grant from the Consolidated Fund, and without interfering with the present manag•ment. LOCAL GOVERNMENT, The Reform of Local Government is now advocated by Lord Saiisbury, who tells us he has always been hi favour. of decentralisation; but the party which mutilated the Municipal Corporation Acts in 1825 by the int, eduction of non-elected members, under the name of aldermen, and who have always shown an inAluctive dread of popular election, are not to be trusted with the conduct of this great Reform, which can only be successfully carried out by a Liberal Government. Jam glad to notice that Mr. Gladstone says that the the first ebje;t to be aimed at is to rectify the balance of taxation as betwe•n real and personal property, and to Put an and to the gross injustice of charging upon labour, through the medium of the Consolidated Fund, local bur- dens which our laws have always wisely treated as incident to property. To the new County Councils I would'grant full'powers of control over Licenses for the sale of sic .holic liquors, but should the measure proposed not include such powers. I shall be prepared to give my support to any well-devised scheme of Local Option. IRELAND. With respect to Ireland, which mast necessarily engage the attention of the coming Parliament, I have always sysipathis,d with the aspirations of her people to- wards Rome Rule, and have consistently depre.mted a policy of coercion. I agree with Mr. John Morley, that a separation would bee disaster to Ireland and a disgrace to England, but. I firmly believe in order to bring ab rut a true union of the Kingdoms, which exists now only in aame, we should grant to Ireland as much self-government as is consistent with the integrity of the empire. As a Past President of the Liverpool Chamber of Com- merce, and Chairman of the Widnes Traders and other- Commercial Associations, I trust that if returned to Par- liament by your suffrages, I shall be able to be of come service to the industrial and commercial intereits ot the community which I shall have the honour to represent. I am, Gentlemen, Your faithful Servant,. EDMUND R. MUBPRATT.

TO THE ELECTORS OF THE PARLIAMENTARY BOROII4II OF BT. HELENS GRETLEMEN,—I congratulate you that, for the first time you are now about to have direct representation in the Im- perial Parliament. I have, as you know, been all my life associated with the progress of Bt. Helens. I was one of the promoters of the first Improvement Act, and sat, for. many years, as a Commis- stoner ; I also took an active part in the movement for In- corporation, and. since the grant of the Cbarter, have acted continuously on the Council; and it is, therefore, with peculiar pleasure that I now see the Town elevated to the Anal dignity of a Parliamentary Borough St. Helens certainly deserves and ought to make good use of Parliamentary Representation. It not only has a large and increasing population, but the products of many of its Indus- tries are the subjecfe of Commercial Treaties with other Coun- tries ; and it cannot but be useful. when such Treaties are under discussion in the House of Commons, that someone should be that e directly authorised to speak on your behalf, ard, if possible, practically acquainted with every disadvant age under which your enterprise labours. It is not less important that the representative of a commu- nity for which Free Trade has done so much should be, as I am, from experience and by conviction, an unflinching Free Trader. On these grounds it is, I suppose, next to their knocledge of my polikic,si views, that the Liberal Association of the Borough have acted in requesting me to become to become their candidate. I can, ao all events, honestly .ay that, in becoming such candidate, and in now appealing to you for your support, I am animated by the hope that, if returned to Parliament as your representative—in addition to supporting the party ot my political attachment—l may be able, with something like efficiency, directly to represent the special in- terests of a town and trade which are equally yours and aims. In Politics, I am and always have been a Liberal. If a Member of the House wf Commons, I should have Duo- ported in the past, as lam prepared to support in the future, what I regard as the enlightened policy of Mr. Gladst ,ne. None but his mast eoleuius could honourably have extricated us frem the legacy of foreign entanglements which the Liberal party inherited in 1880; and, although the process has been slow and paint il and costly, we can rejoice to-day that we are (as I earnestly hops we may long continue) at peace with all the World lam jealous of all initial Interests; but I becieve, in the words or Lord Derby, that ''the first ef British Interests is Peace;" and tarn firmly coovinced that In the eonservation of our present splendid Empire, and in abstention from all controversies not our own, lie the best hopes of our continuous moral and material ascendancy in the seers! of Nations. At home, tarn in favour, first of all. of reforming the pro- oedure of the House of Commons it.elf, on the gene al lines wh eb Mr. Gladstone has lately laid down in his published address to his constituents I am also in favour of freeing the land of our Riogdom from all artifielal barriers to the operation of the laws of ouppl and Demand. I would, therefore rigorously restrict the rignt to create Entails, and entirely abolish the oust, an of Primogeni- ture • and. in addition, ebdeavour to make the Tran fer of Lard as simple and inexpetsive as the Transfer of Government Stock. I am oppesed to the Disentablishment of the English Church; arid I am not willing to give up the existing right of all Denominations to impart Religious Instruction in Ll-mentary Cchools, which have not only seen erected and largely sup. ported by them, but are principall attended by their own children. lam convinced, however, that this cherished principle may be stric,ly maintained under the system of Free Eduoation, or which lam in favour ; which simply mooosts, by openi .g Mt Elementary Soho. ls without lees, to compensate in is me degree the working - classes oi our country for the Eodowed Bey,ools and Colleges which have been but too completely lost to them. Voluntary Schools would thus .be put upon an equal footing in this im- portant matter with Board Schools. and their managers and teachers, without any turtber interference than the existing sucervision of the Education Department, be enabled to shire with the scholars and their parems the great relief from an- noyance and anxiety which the present system inflicts all round. On the larger subject of the whole condition of Edu- cation th, oughout the country, I and entirely in favour of the appointment of a Royal Commission, which has been sug- gested with the view of placing the schools provided by volun- tary efforts on a basis of just and permanent equality with those erected by School Boards. Closely allied to these questions of Religion and Education is that of the control of the Liquor Traffic. This, I believe. ought practically to be in the hands of the people; and, if the necessary provision be not made in the anticipated Local Gov- ernment Bill, I shall vote. if in Parliament, for any well-con- sidered independent legislation on so important a subject Extended Local Goverement both for Great Britain and Ire- land would have my warm support. The large number of Local Authorities now frequently existing in one and the same District are fruitful causes of expense and irritation ; while one Board for a Town or a Division of a County would, in my opinion, be able to perform,muck more efficiently an 6 tar more cheaply than is the case at present, the various duties now entrusted to Town Councils, Local Boards. Burial Boards, Boards of Guardians, and other rate-laying .Authort- ties. In Ireland. having regard to its geographical position as well as to other considerations, something wider than this may be be needed. What is known as" Castle Rule" is already con- demned ; and, in making concession to the desire for a really responsible share in the management of affairs so strongly possessing the pubic men of Ireland. I would (to quote Mr. Gladstone) "dismiss every fear except that of doing wrong." I am an Irishman myself; and, as such, I dmire to see my Country peaceful and prosperous, and in firm and natural alli- ance with Great Britain. The other subjects of a Domestic Character which, in my opinion, are fully ripe for legislation principally cow:sewn the werking classes. First among them. I put the Laws for the Registration of Voters; the reform of which, in the direction of simplicity and certainty. I regard as the necessary cem- plement of the Franchise and Redistribution Acts, th- Ballot Act, the Corrupt Practices Acts, and the Act for Extending the Hours of Polling—all passed by the: Liberal Party. lam also convinced that the provisions of the Employers' Liability Aot ought to be made compulsory; and I approve of the proposed alteration in the Mines Re ulation Act tor securing more corn. pkely the right of the Miners t s choose their own Cheek- weighmen. The aim which I set before myself, as to these and kindred torce, too numerous to mention here. is that the interests of Labour and Capital may be so reconciled as to avoid the ims and disturbance inevitably attendant upon trade disputes, and that the Indastries of the ,Country ma. be thus enabled to hold that rank In the Markets at the World which has so long been pre-eminently theirs I am strongly averse to all taxation on the Necessaries of Life, and to the taxation, under any guise. of persons only earning a nrcessary Lvellhood. Property must be made to heir a juster share of Taxation than it now coee, in relief of the too heavy burdens at present falling on the Industrial and Middle Classes. In this connection. TO THE ELECTORS OF THE NEWTON DIVISION OF LAN CASH I RE. GENTLEMES,—BiII months have now passed since the com- mittees of the Liberal party did me the ^.-nonr of inviting me to become the candidate, in the Liberal interest, for the New- ton Division of Lancashire, where I have resided the greater past of my life. Should you confirm this expression of mitdenee in me by securing my election fur your Division, under the operation of the New Franchise Act, it will be my endeavour to devote my Urns, and such experience as I possess, is. the furtherance of the best interests of the great Liberal cause. tor by conviction I belong to the party that rev-Anises; Mr. Gladstone as its leader, and believing that the views which occupy a prominent position in his "Manifesto," are best cal- culated to promote the welfare of the nation at large, and those sections of the community in whose behalf legislation seems to me to be specially needed, I should give my hearty support to the measures which that Illustrious states- man has advocated. Having from my earliest years been a member of the Church either under the form estabiisbed in ISeotlacd. et* umder that of the Church of England, I deprecate any attempt to sever the connection between Church and State, which has so long existed to the benefit of religion and to the blessing of the people. At the same time I should be glad to further any salutary reforms whereby the National Church should be the better able to discharge her duties to the people. And, as heretofore during my whole life. I am anxious to see and to encourage healthy yet charitable emulation between the vari- ous Christian denominations and the Estatairied Church. I thoroughly approve of the proposal to institute County Boards, as being in the nature of things best qualified to dis- charge local busin-ss, wi,h due regard to L Interest, with more promptitude and efficiency than can be •.pected from the Imperial Parliament. The present system of granting and with-holding Licenses is generally admitted to be unsatisfac- tory ad detective, sand it is believed that a ..inty Board, with its knowledge of the wants of the neighN. ,rhood, would be well qualifisd to grant Licenses in future, aer. well as to have the power of with-holding them. I trust that the present system of education conducted in our denominational schools will not be disturbed. but I would like to see some change in the manner of assisting those parents who are unable to pay the fees. I believe that all agree in the necessity of altering the laws affecting land. It shou:d be made as free and t. ansterable as that of any commodity. It is anticipatel that the changes will be beneficial alike dire2tly to the landowner, the tenant, the farm labourer, and I believe, by the increased productive- ness of the soil, indirectly to the country at large. The time cannot be far distant when the reform of the House f Lords must be carefully brought forwaid so as to prevent the Hens:Mary Chamber from thwarting the well-considered decisions of the Representative Chamber, the Commons House of Parliament. I have always been heartily in favour of Free Trade, aud would oppose any return to a policy of Protec' ion. It shall be my anxious desire to watch carefully over the interests of Agriculture and Trade, and the safety and well- being of our Miners and Sailors, to whose courage and indus- try we are largely indebted for much of the prosperity and wealth of the Empire. as well as the comfort of the whole community, and their oti upations being attended with con- siaerable risk, fresh legislation in their /- shall is demands-f. I consider the efficiency of the Army and Navy all-important for the protection of our Country and Colonies, but not fer unnecessary interference with Foreign Nations. Deploring as I do the troubles and sufferings that still pre- vail in Ireland, I am prepared to cordially welcome and sup- port such good measures as may be brought forward in the interest of our fellow-countrymen, who are certainly entitled to all the privileges which are enjoy ed by the rest of the United Kingdom. Antic pating the carrying out of these and other important men-urea, I approve of amending the rules of the Rouse of Commons so as to prevent obstruction and secure the proper discussion and consideration of ell subjects that may be brought under its notice There are other topics that will require attention, and as I expect shortly to have the pleasure of meeting you in the various Districts of the Division, we shall have opportu- -Aties of exchanging our views regarding all important measures. In conclusion I will only briefly state that my aim, if I should be so fortut ate as to obtain your suffrages, will be to labour for the best interests of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Irelmd and our Colonies, without losing sight of those special claims upon my loyal service which would de- volve upon me as your liepresentative. I have the honour to be, Gentlemen, Your faithful Servant, GEOttGE McCORQUOD ILK. The Willows, Newton-le-Willows, October 20th, 1085.

_ WIT AND HUMOUR. Why is an umbrella like yesterday P—Because, once gone, it never returns. • It is a wise provision of nature, that a man can neither kick himself nor pat his own back. The curious man will know everything that his wife carries in her pocket, but the wise one tries not to know that she has one. N 'ACURA —BUT AFTER?—" How can I find oat all about the young lady to whom I am engaged ?" asked a prospec- tive Benedict. "The simplest way would be to marry her," answered his friend. IT DEPENDED ON CIRCUBISTANCES.—FriVOIOUS young lady, to guide: How deep is this hole P—Guide : Never been measured, num.—Frivolous young lady: Suppose I were to fall down there, where do you suppose I should go to P—Guide :That depends, miss, upon how you have lived in this world! MATSIMONIAL FELICITY. Theopholis Hitchkiss, of Waco, married a second time, and, as is often the case, he and his wife disagree. "I am sorry, Jane, that I did not become acquainted with you before I was a widower." "Why so?" she asked with surprise. "Because some other woman would be mY wife now," he replied with a sigh. Daughter (home from school) : Now, pa, are you satis- fied? Just look at my testimonial—" Political economy, satisfactory; fine arts and music, very good; logic, excel- lent."--Fither : Very much so, my dear—especially as regards your future. If your husband should understand anything of housekeeping, cooking, mending, and the use of a sewing machine, perhaps your married life will indeed be happy- A lady in Detroit advertised for a servant, and a coloured woman put in an appearance. Her first question was, "Has yer got any chillun ?" "No, I have no children. Why do you ask ?" " Bekase, if yes hain't got no chillun, I hain't gwinter stay avid yer." "What have children to do with your work ?" "I don't wanter stay in no house whar dar's no chillun, bekase den, wheneber any dishes am broke, it am always laid on de servant and tucken oaten her wages." WHERE ris was AT HOME.—Jim Webster was brought up before an Austin justice of the peace. It was the s.me charge that used to bother him in Galveston. After the evidence was all in, the judge, with a perplexed look, said, "But I do not comprehend, Webster, how it MO possible for you to steal those fowls when they were roosting right under the owner's window, and there were two vicious dogs in the yard." "Hit wouldn't do yer a bit of good, jedge, for me to 'splain how I cotched dem chickens, for yer couldn't do hit yerself if yer tried forty times, and yer might get yer hide full of buckshot de berry fast these yer put yer leg ober de fence. Da best way fur you to do, jedge, is fur yer to buy yer chickens in de market, like uder folks, and, when yer wants ter commit any rascality, do hit on de bench, whar you am at home !" A visitor at a restaurant noticed that the waiter invariably put the coppers into his waistcoat pocket, and when giving Out change he was always a penny or two short, With the natural consequence that the guests made him a present of the small change. When our visitor came to settle his account this manoeuvre was repeated; but he said to the waiter, "Just feel in your waistcoat pocket!" to which the astonished garcon replied with a smile, "Been a waiter your- self, sometime, I suppose ?" SHE NEVES TALKED SLANG.—The typical Chicago girl, who is known all over the Unitei States as the possessor of the largest feet in America, has been cruelly libelled. A Boston paper recently declared that she habitually talked slang, and made use of such expressions as " getting left," "corralled a handkerchief," and put Millis best licks." A reporter at once called upon a representative Chicago young lady, WhO belengale One Of the firet families of that city, and asked her what she thought of the assertion. " This hi a fish story," she replied, with natural indignation. " The fellow who wrote it is 'way off his base. There may be some of us who sling slang; but I never work the slang racket' myself—not this child! Now you hear my bauoo !We can discount Boston on beauty; and, as for accomplishments, why, that's where we hold a full hand! Take me for ex- ample. I can paw the ivory; I can warble a few warts; and I can elocute. Boston girls are just disgruntled. The fact is they have got to hustle to keep even with us; and don't smu forget it !" This interview seems to have effectually Nettled the Vestion. The libellous Boston paper should now apologise. A farmer who had lost some COWS by the eattle-plague was folly persuaded that he had himself been attacked by the epidemic. Forthwith he consulted his medical man, who tried to laugh him out of his notion, but to no purpose. The farmer then went off to an old well-knoWn practitioner, who, being a bit of a wag, and seeing how matters stood, entered minutely into the details of the case, expressed his concurrence with the patient's views, and told him he could cure him. He then wrote a prescription, sealed it up, and told the farmer to go to a certain druggist in the next town. The farmer lost no time in going with the prescription, but was somewhat startled when the druggist showed him the formula, which ran thus—" This man has got the cattle- plague; take him into the back-yard and shoot him, ac- cording to Act of Parliament." The happy result was a " perfect cure." On the placards which advertised a walk against time at Lillie Bridge the pedestrian was depicted striding along in advance of Father Time, who was represented as an old man, armed and clad in the usual metaphorical manner. During I the afternoon of the " walk " a rough member of the" fancy" demanded of the gatekeeper the return of his "bob." "What's the matter ?" said the official. "You have been here for four hours to my knowledge, and you have seen him I walk !" That's true," replied the rough ; "but I came to see that cove with the scythe, and he hasn't turned up ; and II mean to have my money back; so out with it and no bloomin"umbug !"

Egl Spencer spoke at Harleston, on Friday, in favour of co-operative farming. A telegram from Baronscourt on Friday says the Duke of Abercorn is sinking from exhaustion. Mr. Gladstone visited Earl Granville on Friday morning, and returned to Harwarden in the afternoon. A 'Times" telegram, dated Assouan Friday, says a large rebel army has left Omdurman for Abbamad. At Dover, on Friday afternoon, six men, charged with robbing Government storesovere committed for trial. The Earl of Beckinghamshire died on Thursday evening at Hampden Hamm, Bucks, aged 92, having been born on November let, 1793. His eldest son is Hobart Pasha, THE Etnerrox.—Staffordshire authorities, having ex- cellent reasons for belieYing that writs will be in their hands on November 18th, have fixed nomination and polling days for the Yarioaa divisions. The International Arbitration Association have sent a memorial to Her Majesty in council praying for the re- prieve of Louis Riel ; but from the answer received it appears that the decision rests with the Canadian authori- ties Tame ARMSTRONG AnnucrioN CAM—The Armstrong case was reenmed at the Old Bailey on Friday, before Mr. Jus- tice Lopes, who announced that the Court would at rising adjourn till Monday.—Mrs. Jarrett was further examined by Mr. C. Matthews, and swore she never heard Mrs. Arm- strong say she would not let her daughter go for immoral purposes. Answering Mr. Stead, she admitted he told her not to seek for fresh girls, but only those in stock.—Mr. Justice Lopes told Mr. Stead this did not help his defence. He might have been actuated by high-minded, honourable, and philanthropic motives, but the question was whether the law had been broken. CAPTURE OF BURGLARS.—A POLICEMAN SHOT DEAD. Further particulars have come to hand of the capture of some of the burglars concerned in the daring robbery at Netherbv Hall, near Carlise, on Wednesday night. The , four burglars were seen by a goods guard on the railway to enter a wagon on his train near Penrith. The guard threw off a note at Shari to be wired forward to Tebay. This was done, and on arriving at Tebay several railway men with the guard surrounded the wagon. One of the burglars presented a revolver over the side of the wagon, and swore he would shoot anyone who tried to arrest them. He, how- ever, was promptly disabled by the stationmaster of Tebay, who struck the ruffian on the head with a brakestick, and he was secured, together with one of his companions. The other two scrambled out of the wagon, and managed to make their escape, although pursued for a considerable dis- tance by the railway men. The body of a policeman, evi- dently shot dead by the desperadoes, has been found thrown over a hedge near Carlisle. THE- ATTEMPTED ASSASSINATION OF M. DE FREYCINET. The man who attempted to assassinate M. de Freycinet is now said to be a Corsican named Maltei. He had pre- viously called at the Foreign Office and demanded an inter- view in order to obtain redress. M. de Freycinet is posi- tive he had never seen the man before or heard of his ro- gues'. He is supposed to be insane. THE EASTERN CRISIS. BELORADE, FRlDAY.—Servian commanders on the Bul- garian frontier have been ordered to answer by force any further provocation by the Bulgarians without waiting for orders from heacl•quarters. THE .BURMAH DIFFICULTY. Several officers belonging to the British Army in India. at present in England on leave, have been ordered to rejoin their regiments at once for service in Burmah. , Several left London by the Indian mail on Friday evening, and many others will go next we.k.
